Iran accused France of "violent treatment" of the protesters and "extensive and flagrant human rights violations" during the demonstrations, which began late last month and have been accompanied by unrest.
Relations between France and Iran have been strained for months, with the two expelling each other's diplomats in August.
Iran itself suffered major anti-government protests in January, during which the authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, blaming "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs maintain that security forces fired on protesters.
Most families of U.S. troops killed in the Iran war's deadliest attack to skip White House event
Most families of the in the deadliest attack of the Iran war will not be attending a major White House event for Gold Star families hosted by President Trump.
Only one family member of those killed in an Iranian drone strike March 1 on confirmed to The Associated Press that they planned to attend Tuesday's reception with Mr. Trump and the first lady.

"I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency."
Some Gold Star families say they are grateful for how the Trump administration and military have honored their loved one's sacrifice. Other families say the way the White House has handled the reception is the latest indication that the administration does not respect the price they have paid.
The spouse of Maj. Alex Klinner, an airman who was killed in an Iran-related combat operation this summer, said receiving less than two weeks' notice did not give her enough time to arrange for overnight care for her three young children.
In a text message, Libby Klinner said she would not have gone anyway, adding, "I have no interest in supporting an administration that has been so reckless with the lives of our service members."
The war, launched Feb. 28, has claimed the lives of 19 U.S. troops and wounded more than 800 others.

The Houthis were fighting Tuesday around Dhubab, a strategic town in Yemen that its internationally-recognized government had previously said it had retaken, a senior Yemeni military official told The Associated Press. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.
Joined by its Yemeni government allies, Saudi Arabia is leading a coalition to attack Houthi military targets in Yemen. Their offensive follows the government's announcement on Sunday, declaring a campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territories in the country. Fighting has been concentrated in a region near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil and gas exports.

Saudi Arabia says forces intercepted Houthi missile targeting country's southwest
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said on Tuesday that its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at a city in Saudi Arabia's southwest.
The coalition's spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said on X that it "intercepted and destroyed" the missile launched towards Khamis Mushait, which is home to an air base.

"Bessent's delusional forecasts never had any credibility in the first place. His latest propaganda will have an equally short shelf life," Rezaei wrote on X.
He added: "You lost the military war. You will fail in the economic war, too. Hormuz will not be opened by threats or pressure. Iran will not back down."

At a campaign rally in Nebraska, Mr. Trump called the Iran war "artificial," but added that he wanted to see a "total victory." He suggested the war was a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe."
"They can take out a city," Mr. Trump said, alluding to the risk of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego."
Attendees cheered after his remark. It was not immediately clear what Mr. Trump meant, but the comments were quickly condemned by California Gov. Gavin Newsom and other state officials.

"He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung argued. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."

The Iranian nationals visited addresses linked to people including two journalists working for the Farsi-language television network, which Tehran has long labeled a terror organization.

articles.title: The day the fault lines cracked: October 7’s aftershocks travelled from Israel and Gaza to Iran, Red Sea a - The Economic Times
articles.summary: The day the fault lines cracked: October 7’s aftershocks travelled from Israel and Gaza to Iran, Red Sea a  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The aircraft plunges. Passengers and crew scramble to overpower him. Another pilot eventually takes control.
Everyone makes it out alive.
Also Read: War-weary Israelis rethink loyalty to Netanyahu before election
That was flydubai flight FZ1073 last week. UAE authorities have called the incident a "terrorist attack". Israeli officials later told Reuters that the co-pilot allegedly planned the attack before joining the airline, while another source briefed on the UAE investigation said he intended to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion Airport.
Tens of thousands have been killed. Cities have been reduced to rubble. Ships have abandoned one of the world's busiest trade routes. Israel and Iran have gone from fighting largely through proxies and covert operations to firing directly at each other. American forces have struck Iranian nuclear sites. Oil has crossed $100 a barrel.
A war that started along a strip of land on the Mediterranean eventually reached the world's shipping lanes, energy markets and major capitals.
October 7, 2023
It began on a Saturday morning.
Hamas-led militants broke through the Gaza border into southern Israel, attacking communities, military positions and the Nova music festival.
By the end of the attack, about 1,200 people had been killed. Another 251 were dragged back into Gaza as hostages: civilians and soldiers, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals.
For Israel, October 7 became the deadliest day in the country's history and exposed a security failure that would haunt its politics and military establishment for years.
Israel responded by going to war in Gaza.
Also Read: How October 7 reshaped Israelis’ relationship with Judaism, faith and tradition
By October 2026, about 74,000 Palestinians had been killed in the Israeli campaign, according to Gaza health authorities, whose figures are cited by Reuters and AP. The health ministry does not distinguish between civilians and combatants in its overall count.
Israel says it targets Hamas and seeks to minimise civilian casualties. It has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating among civilians and using civilian infrastructure for military purposes. Hamas has denied some of those allegations.
Much of Gaza was devastated. Homes disappeared, hospitals struggled to function and most of the territory's population was displaced during the fighting.
Then came another enemy: hunger.
In August 2025, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, the global hunger monitor used by UN agencies and aid groups, determined that famine was occurring in parts of Gaza. It estimated 514,000 people were experiencing famine conditions.
Israel rejected the finding as false and biased.
By then, however, Gaza was no longer the only place living with the consequences of October 7.
The war crossed the border
On October 8, 2023, Iran-backed Hezbollah began firing at Israeli military positions from Lebanon, saying it was acting in support of Hamas.
For months, Israel and Hezbollah traded fire across the border. Then the conflict widened dramatically.
Your package from Asia to Europe suddenly had a longer journey
That same year, the Houthis in Yemen entered the conflict from the other end of the Arabian Peninsula.
The Iran-backed group began attacking vessels in the Red Sea, saying it was acting in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
That mattered well beyond the Middle East.
The Red Sea leads to the Suez Canal, one of the shortcuts that keeps global commerce moving. Shut or threaten that route and ships travelling between Asia and Europe have an unpleasant alternative: sail all the way around Africa.
That is exactly what major shipping companies began doing.
Journeys became longer. Ships burned more fuel. Freight and insurance costs rose. Delivery schedules changed.
Suddenly, an attack that began at the Gaza border was being felt in global supply chains.
Israel and Iran step out of the shadows
Israel and Iran had been enemies for decades, but much of their confrontation played out indirectly: through covert operations, cyberattacks and armed groups backed by Tehran.
That barrier began to crumble after October 7.
Iran fired hundreds of drones and missiles directly at Israel in April 2024 following a strike on Tehran's diplomatic compound in Damascus that Iran and Syria blamed on Israel. Israel later retaliated.
Then came June 2025.
Israel struck Iranian military and nuclear targets during a 12-day war. Iran responded with waves of missiles and drones.
And then the United States joined in.
American forces bombed Iranian nuclear facilities before a US-brokered ceasefire ended that round of fighting.
A conflict that began with Hamas gunmen entering southern Israel had, less than two years later, helped push Israel and Iran into direct war and drawn the world's most powerful military into the confrontation.
Enter Donald Trump
Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 with Gaza still unresolved.
Within weeks, he stunned allies and adversaries by proposing that the United States take over Gaza and redevelop it after Palestinians were resettled elsewhere. Arab governments rejected the idea.
His administration then pursued talks over Iran's nuclear programme while simultaneously trying to secure a Gaza settlement.
In September 2025, Trump won Benjamin Netanyahu's backing for a 20-point Gaza proposal. Israel and Hamas subsequently agreed to its first phase, producing a ceasefire, hostage releases, the freeing of Palestinian prisoners and an initial Israeli military withdrawal.
Trump travelled to Israel the following month and addressed the Knesset.
For a moment, the Middle East appeared to have stepped back from the edge.
It hadn't.
Then came the oil shock
By 2026, the US and Israel were again at war with Iran.
This time, one of the world's most important pieces of water was caught in the middle.
The Strait of Hormuz is narrow enough to look almost insignificant on a world map. Economically, it is anything but. Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption traditionally passes through the waterway.
Disrupt it and the effects don't stay in Tehran, Tel Aviv or Washington.
They reach petrol pumps.
Iran's effective blockade of Hormuz forced Gulf producers to find alternative export routes. Tankers faced sharply higher insurance and freight costs. Governments released emergency oil reserves.
Saudi Arabia moved crude through its East-West pipeline towards the Red Sea.
Then that escape route came under pressure too.
Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in July helped push Brent crude above $100 a barrel as markets contemplated something once difficult to imagine: disruption simultaneously threatening both of the Middle East's major maritime energy routes.
Reuters reported that tanker freight rates on some Middle East-to-Asia routes jumped from around $30,000 to as much as $1.2 million a day.
At that point, October 7 and it’s aftershocks had entered shipping bills, inflation calculations and energy prices.
One day, three years of aftershocks
It would be too simple to say October 7 created every conflict that followed.
Israel and Iran were enemies long before 2023. Hezbollah's confrontation with Israel goes back decades. Yemen's war produced the Houthis long before Gaza returned to the centre of global attention. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict itself stretches back generations.
But October 7 struck those fault lines.
It shattered Israel's sense of security and triggered a war that devastated Gaza. Hezbollah opened another front. The Red Sea became dangerous for commercial shipping. Israel and Iran began attacking each other directly. Washington found itself pulled back into another Middle Eastern war. Hormuz became a threat to the world's oil supply.

articles.title: Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means  Al JazeeraSaudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey trigger mutual defence pact  Financial TimesPakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey Trigger Mutual Defense Pact Over Houthi Attacks  Foreign PolicyPakistan Says Mecca Pact Is Supporting Saudi Arabia With Houthis  Bloomberg.comTurkey and Pakistan pledge to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia  Le Monde.fr
articles.full_text:
Islamabad, Pakistan — For the first time since it was signed in August, the Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye is now in force.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the pact’s top committee agreed to deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, which is backing an offensive against Yemen’s Houthis.
“The Committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the Parties,” said a joint statement shared by Pakistan’s Foreign Office.
The statement did not specify the size or role of the forces.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were supporting a counteroffensive by the internationally recognised Yemeni government to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.
Hours after the meeting, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part.
“The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role. We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces, and they are the ones retaking those areas,” Asif told Geo News, speaking from Riyadh on Monday night.
That leaves Pakistan in a defensive role alongside a Saudi offensive. Analysts told Al Jazeera that it raises a question Islamabad has yet to answer publicly: How long can it stay out of the actual fighting?
What is already in place?
Pakistan already had a military presence in Saudi Arabia. It has trained Saudi military personnel since 1967, with a 1982 agreement formalising the deputation of troops to the kingdom.
A declassified CIA assessment from June 1985 estimated that 13,000 to 14,000 Pakistanis were serving in the Saudi army, including an armoured brigade at Tabuk. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, Pakistan also sent a large contingent to the kingdom for defensive duties.
Pakistan also signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia in September 2025, which treats aggression against either country as aggression against both.
In April, Riyadh confirmed that a Pakistani force, including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the Eastern Province.
Pakistan has not disclosed how many of its troops are in Saudi Arabia.
In September, Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), told the Saudi outlet Arab News that Pakistani forces were already deployed to protect the kingdom and its holy sites.
“I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.”
ISPR did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the deployment agreed upon in Riyadh.
On Tuesday, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said in a post on X that the country’s commitment to the security of the holy sites and the kingdom was not negotiable.
“The operational details of the actualisation of the collective deterrence are a matter of operational confidentiality and may not be made subject of media speculation,” the ministry said.
Turkiye’s footprint is less clear.
Asif said Turkish forces were also present, but Ankara has not publicly confirmed any deployment.
“There is no publicly acknowledged standing Turkish deployment in Saudi Arabia,” Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera.
Ereli noted that under Article 92 of Turkiye’s constitution, the authority to send troops abroad rests with the parliament, which has yet to ratify the Mecca pact.
What could deterrence look like?
Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum, said Riyadh wants the pact to carry real weight.
“Saudi Arabia is trying to turn the Mecca pact from a political declaration into a deterrent,” she told Al Jazeera.
For now, she said, Riyadh mainly wants Pakistan and Turkiye to help defend Saudi territory and reinforce its air and missile defences, showing that another attack is no longer only a Saudi-Houthi matter. The Houthis have attacked multiple Saudi cities and facilities, including the East-West Pipeline that Riyadh has been using to export oil amid Iranian restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz during the ongoing war waged by the US.
Saudi authorities said two airports in the kingdom had been hit on Monday evening, injuring at least three people.
But Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman’s account of the meeting went further than what Thafer suggested.
“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” he wrote on X.
Thafer said the wording was deliberate.
“‘All those responsible’ is intentionally ambiguous. It tells the Houthis that Saudi Arabia may go beyond intercepting missiles and strike any actor or infrastructure enabling those attacks. It is also simultaneously warning external sponsors that Riyadh is watching the entire support network,” she said.
However, Pakistani officials have been more cautious.
“The document itself says, first, that it is defensive in nature. It has no offensive agenda,” Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said at a news conference in Islamabad on October 2.
Tughral Yamin, a retired brigadier and senior associate at Islamabad’s Institute of Policy Studies, said Pakistan’s contribution was likely to be specialised rather than large.
“Pakistan is most likely going to beef up its existing presence with air defence units, drones, battlefield communication systems and offensive cyber specialists, men from the corps of engineers to lay and lift mines, some special service troops. Nothing more than that, I would say,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ereli expects Turkiye’s role to be similarly limited.
“The realistic response would be calibrated and mostly non-ground. That means diplomatic coordination, intelligence sharing, emergency resupply of air defence, drones and electronic warfare, and perhaps naval or air-defence assets,” he said.
Could it extend into Yemen?
Thafer said two campaigns were now running side by side.
“There are really two concentric operations taking place: one is defending Saudi Arabia; the second is changing the military balance inside Yemen so the Houthis cannot continue attacking Saudi territory from a position of growing strength,” she said.
Pakistan has not said publicly where its role stops.
Asked by reporters in Rome on September 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, Asif did not answer directly.
“I’m not going into detail, but obviously, when I say that we are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia, that means whatever means are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” he said.
Pakistan has faced this question before.
In April 2015, its parliament unanimously resolved that “Pakistan should maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”. But the resolution also pledged that Pakistan would stand with Saudi Arabia if its territorial integrity were violated or the holy sites threatened.
Monday’s joint statement justified the deployment in similar terms and condemned the attempted targeting of Mecca and Medina.
Tehran, though, is watching closely. On Sunday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for war in Yemen were untrue. He warned that any new intervention would only complicate the situation.
At the same news conference last week, Dar said he had raised the pact with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in New York in September, on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly.
“I made them aware that we are in a defence pact, and as Muslims, we have to honour it, and God willing, we will,” he said.
He said the Iranian leaders had suggested engaging the Houthis politically rather than through military action. Monday’s statement made no mention of a political track.
Javad Heiran-Nia, an analyst with the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran draws a clear distinction between defending Saudi territory and infrastructure and attacking the Houthis in Yemen.
“In general, if Pakistan’s deployment is purely defensive and limited to the protection of Saudi installations, Tehran can tolerate it. However, if Pakistan joins offensive operations against the Houthis, Iran regards it as a red line, since it views the Houthis as part of its strategic depth in the Arabian Peninsula,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Currently, Pakistan’s mediation has shifted from neutrality to management of conflicting interests, and its credibility is highly fragile,” he added.
Institute of Policy Studies’ Yamin, too, said the onus was on Islamabad.
“Pakistan needs to draw its red lines carefully to prevent its troops [from] getting involved in combat operations against the Houthis. So the question should [be] not how will they get involved but how can they prevent getting involved,” he said.
How long will it last?
Much depends on what Riyadh wants from Yemen.
“Riyadh probably wants a short, high-intensity campaign that restores deterrence rather than another open-ended Yemen war,” Thafer said.
But Yemeni government forces this week said they were no longer limiting their ambitions to regaining territory lost to the Houthis in recent weeks, and were in fact aiming to retake the capital, Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed group since 2014.

articles.title: $2.5bn NEOM Sky Stadium Shelved as 46,000-seat Saudi Arabia's World Cup Project Loses Momentum - Construction Review
articles.summary: $2.5bn NEOM Sky Stadium Shelved as 46,000-seat Saudi Arabia's World Cup Project Loses Momentum  Construction Review
articles.full_text:
NEOM Sky Stadium plans have been shelved indefinitely, removing one of Saudi Arabia’s most ambitious proposed World Cup venues. The $2.5 billion stadium formed part of The Line, NEOM’s futuristic 160-kilometre development. The proposed venue would have seated more than 46,000 spectators.
Its pitch was planned more than 350 meters above ground level. However, delays and downsizing across The Line have changed the stadium’s construction outlook. Two sources familiar with the project confirmed its indefinite suspension to Reuters.
NEOM Sky Stadium construction plans hit The Line setback
NEOM Sky Stadium was designed as a signature sports landmark within The Line. Saudi Arabia’s official World Cup plans identify the project as NEOM Stadium. The “Sky Stadium” description reflects its extraordinary elevated design.
The stadium would have featured a pitch positioned more than 350 meters above ground. Its roof would have formed part of the surrounding city structure. Furthermore, the design aimed to create an integrated sports venue within The Line.
The proposed capacity stood at 46,010 spectators. The venue would have hosted group-stage and knockout matches during the 2034 World Cup. Those stages included the round of 32, round of 16 and quarter-final.
Initially, Saudi Arabia expected the stadium to reach completion by 2032. The venue also formed part of the country’s original 15-stadium World Cup proposal.
However, the stadium depended heavily on The Line’s wider construction program. That development has subsequently faced major delays and significant scope reductions.
NEOM Sky Stadium construction stalls alongside wider giga-project changes
NEOM Sky Stadium construction now faces an uncertain future after The Line lost priority. Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan confirmed that shift earlier this year. He also said The Line was not essential before its original 2030 target.
Nevertheless, Al-Rumayyan previously denied that Saudi Arabia had cancelled projects. The latest stadium decision therefore represents a significant change surrounding the ambitious development.
MEED Projects now lists the proposed stadium as “on hold”. The platform estimates its construction cost at approximately $2.5 billion. It currently provides no completion date for the venue.
The shelving also follows broader changes affecting Saudi Arabia’s expensive giga-project program. FreeYork reported that The Line underwent reviews amid concerns surrounding costs and delivery. Those pressures have contributed to reductions across the wider development.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia continues developing other World Cup construction projects. The country plans 15 venues across five host cities for the 2034 tournament. The overall stadium program carries an estimated value of $22.7 billion.
Saudi Arabia’s changing stadium construction program extends beyond NEOM, with the $20.4 billion Jeddah Central development also featuring a major sports stadium.
The Jeddah project covers 5.7 square kilometres and includes residential, hospitality, cultural and marine facilities. Its planned stadium forms part of five major construction packages that attracted contractor bids.
NEOM Sky Stadium construction leaves World Cup venue strategy evolving
NEOM Sky Stadium construction would have delivered one of the most unconventional football venues ever proposed. Its elevated location would have distinguished it from conventional stadium developments worldwide.
The venue was also intended to continue operating after the tournament. Saudi Arabia planned to make it home to NEOM SC’s professional football teams. It would additionally support sports and active-lifestyle programs within the city.
However, the project now has no confirmed construction schedule. Saudi Arabia’s World Cup authority told Reuters that substantial tournament construction milestones were progressing. It did not specifically address the stadium’s suspension.
Other venues continue moving forward despite the NEOM setback. Aramco Stadium in Al Khobar remains under construction and is expected to reach completion soon.
Saudi Arabia will host the first 48-team World Cup staged entirely within one country. The tournament will therefore require extensive construction, refurbishment and supporting infrastructure.
The NEOM decision highlights the construction risks associated with projects dependent on wider masterplans. Changes to The Line have consequently affected the stadium’s own delivery prospects.
For now, the $2.5 billion NEOM Sky Stadium remains on hold. Its proposed elevated arena has moved from an ambitious World Cup concept to an uncertain construction project.

Saudi Arabia said three people were injured in the latest attacks on its airports since fighting with Yemen's Houthi rebels reignited. Meanwhile, Palestinian officials said Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City killed two people, while condemning home demolitions in east Jerusalem and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Israelis are readying to mark the third anniversary of the Palestinian militant Hamas group's Oct. 7, 2023 attack as conflict in the Middle East has spread to include Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Full coverage is available here.
Saudis say 2 airports were hit
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said airports in the cities of Najran and Jizan were hit on Monday, damaging both facilities and leaving three lightly injured. The statement didn't say who was responsible, but followed an announcement by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels that they fired missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Houthi Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a statement on Tuesday they had fired toward a third airport on Tuesday. The Associated Press could not confirm whether the Houthis had hit Abha International Airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Tuesday it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis toward Khamis Mushait, a city in southwestern Saudi Arabia that's home to a major Saudi military base.
Fighting in Yemen grinds on
The Houthis were fighting Tuesday around Dhubab, a strategic town in Yemen that its internationally recognized government had previously said it had retaken, a senior Yemeni military official told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters.

Saudi Arabia and its allies in Yemen's government have launched a military campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territory near the southern tip of the Red Sea to prevent disruptions to oil being exported out of the region.
By Ahmed al Haj in Aden, Yemen.
Tanker hit in Strait of Hormuz
An outbound tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an "unknown projectile" on Monday, the British military said in a late report Tuesday. There were no immediate reports of casualties or environmental impact.
Even as Iran has lost its near-complete chokehold on the strait, the ongoing risk of Iranian attacks keeps overall ship traffic well below prewar levels.
2 killed in Israeli strike in Gaza
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two people in Gaza City, health officials at the city's Shifa Hospital said. Israel's military said it targeted militants in both strikes.
It was the latest deadly attack since a ceasefire took effect nearly a year ago in the Israel-Hamas war triggered by the 2023 attack, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people, most civilians, in southern Israel and abducted 251 others. More than 1,460 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
Netanyahu warns of potential attack related to Israel's upcoming vote
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday that Hamas could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the country's elections later this month. Netanyahu, who is locked in a tough battle for re-election, did not publicly provide evidence for the claim.
In recent days, Netanyahu's political opponents have pointed to the thwarted FlyDubai cockpit attack as the latest example of his government's failure to manage security threats.
AFP photojournalist says Israeli settlers beat him in olive harvest season attack
Jaafar Ishtyeh, a veteran Palestinian photojournalist for Agence France-Presse, said he was filming the olive harvest in the West Bank village of Aqraba when he heard shooting by Israeli settlers. He said they later encircled him, took his camera as he was filming the attack and beat him, causing injuries that required hospitalization.
The Palestinian Authority said settlers in the area also shot one man in the leg and severely beat two others in the town south of Nablus. Israel's military did not provide immediate comment on the attack.
The attack was the latest this harvest season, during which four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured, according to Palestinian officials.

Israeli authorities tore down a five-story building in east Jerusalem on Tuesday.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir attended the demolition and said that Israeli authorities had demolished more than 10,000 structures built without permits over the past year and a half.
Palestinians say the process of procuring construction permits is nearly impossible for them in east Jerusalem, which Israel annexed in the 1967 Mideast war and is home to almost 400,000 Palestinians.

articles.title: Yemeni troops retake key areas near Bab el-Mandeb from Houthis
articles.summary: Saudi-led coalition forces recaptured several areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said Monday, as the Houthis claimed retaliatory strikes on Sa...
articles.full_text:
Saudi-led coalition forces recaptured several areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said Monday, as the Houthis claimed retaliatory strikes on Saudi oil facilities, airports and military bases.
The Yemeni officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government retook the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait, a vital shipping route that connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.
The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under air cover by a Saudi military coalition.
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesman, claimed in a prerecorded statement that the rebels used ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and an oil refinery in the Red Sea city of Rabigh.
Also attacked were Abha airport, military facilities in Khamis Mushait and other "critical sites" in the cities of Najran and Jizan, he claimed.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory.
Asked if the coalition coordinated the action with the United States, Rubio said that Saudi Arabia and the U.S. have a defense agreement but wouldn’t offer more details.
Since the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by the Houthis and the Saudis have come under attack, "they have a right to defend themselves," Rubio said.
The U.S. has provided support to Saudi Arabia in its ongoing campaign against the Houthis, according to a regional official and a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to reporters. The support included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the offensive, said the officials.
The U.S. had supported the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis early in the Yemen war, before quitting the coalition in recent years.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh warned U.S. citizens on social media to be vigilant about possible drone or missile attacks.
The offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region.
The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to government forces. He said the coalition secured "air protection" of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets.
Also Monday, the foreign and defense ministers of Pakistan and Türkiye agreed with Saudi Arabia to deploy military forces to the kingdom under their defense pact .
A joint statement released by Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry after an emergency meeting in Riyadh did not specify troop numbers, identify which countries would contribute forces or give a deployment timetable.
The three countries condemned what they described as attempted attacks on Mecca and Medina, as well as continuing attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic facilities. The statement did not identify who was responsible.
The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year cease-fire.
Houthis seized the town of Turbah Sunday. Turbah sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for government forces defending Taiz.
Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts, paving the way for the rebels to encircle Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September. They captured the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, through which 12% of global trade transits.
The Saudi-backed government said Sunday it was mobilizing troops across government-held areas.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called on the international community to provide support to his government.
Hours after al-Alimi’s declaration, the Saudi military spokesperson al-Malki vowed "full operational support" to Yemeni government forces until the Houthis are "eliminated."
Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation – dubbed "Yemen Dawn" – had started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" Sanaa, Yemen’s rebel-controlled capital, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup."
Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on Sanaa. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes on their territories, including Sanaa.
The rebels' taking of Turbah will likely constrain government forces’ ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions across Taiz province and the provincial capital of Taiz, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis descended from their northern stronghold, capturing Sanaa and forcing the government to flee into exile in Saudi Arabia. The war created one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters and killed more than 150,000 people.
The latest bout of violence has killed at least 959 people and wounded over 4,200 others, according to the World Health Organization. The flare-up forced about 174,097 people to flee their homes inside Yemen, according to the U.N. migration agency. More than 3,000 others fled across the waters into Djibouti, the agency reported.
Last week, Yemen’s Health Ministry – part of the internationally recognized government – warned about the conflict’s impact on health facilities and medical staff across Taiz province.
The ministry said in a statement on Friday that health facilities in coastal, western and southern areas of the province have closed or are barely partially functioning.

Sustainability, resilience, and security constitute formative pillars of the global energy transition. Given that carbon-intensive fossil fuels yield negative environmental repercussions and face depletion in the long term, hydrogen presents a viable solution to accelerate industrial decarbonisation. Industry accounts for over 21 percent of direct global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, with iron, steel, cement, and chemical sectors comprising 71 percent.[1] Hydrogen’s appeal stems from its versatility as an energy carrier, applicability across multiple end-use segments, and ability to be produced from various sources such as water, fossil fuels, and biomass. These factors underscore its potential as a transitional and clean energy tool.[2]
Hydrogen can fuel power generation and serve as energy storage for renewables. It can also be chemically converted into derivatives, including ammonia and methane, which can be leveraged as feedstock for hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, cement, fertilisers, and chemicals. Compared to other renewables, hydrogen is stable, reliable, and capable of meeting high-temperature requirements to decarbonise such sectors.[3]
Figure 1: Hydrogen Applications: An Overview
Source: BloombergNEF[4]
Initial global interest in hydrogen can be traced to the 2019 Group of Twenty (G20) Summit in Japan which drew attention to it as a key industrial decarbonisation tool.[5] The coinciding launch of the International Energy Agency's (IEA) flagship The Future of Hydrogen report established hydrogen as integral to energy transition. National hydrogen strategies subsequently increased from a small handful to over 30 hydrogen road maps by 2021.[6],[7],[8]
Subsequently, countries such as Japan and Germany attempted to fuel their hydrogen economies through ambitious targets, but encountered geographical, cost, and supply–demand mismatch constraints. Japan, for example, has implemented generous hydrogen subsidies for application in fuel cell passenger vehicles.[9] However, its supply of clean hydrogen is constrained by its geography, as the country is energy-import dependent and lacks land capacity for renewable energy expansion, which has constrained domestic green hydrogen deployment. Other forms of transport decarbonisation, therefore, remain more inexpensive and effective for Japan. Germany’s Hydrogen Import Strategy quantifies projected demand and outlines clear infrastructure linkages, but the country faces similar challenges with hydrogen cost competitiveness, as global demand has fallen short of early expectations.[10]
Despite early positive signalling, the global deployment of clean hydrogen and its derivatives have faced several interrelated challenges, namely, high production costs, infrastructural setbacks, regulatory fragmentation, and lack of secure demand off-takers. Consequently, current global hydrogen progress has fallen short of early established targets. In 2025, Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BNEF) estimated that hydrogen production would rise to 5.5 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) by 2030, well below the 25 mtpa combined global national targets.[11],[12] BNEF’s projections stem from low industry demand for hydrogen as well as technical and cost barriers inhibiting large-scale production and transport.
The prospect of hydrogen development remains attractive and well-suited to Gulf Cooperation Council countries (GCC), which are actively conducting feasibility studies with the aim of establishing commercial-scale hydrogen infrastructure projects.[13] First, the region seeks to diversify its economies away from fossil fuels. Simultaneously, due to increasing climate-related impacts, it is accelerating its decarbonisation efforts. Second, GCC countries are geographically well-positioned, nestled between two key import markets such as Asia and Europe, and boast abundant solar and wind resources. There is also mounting interest in nuclear energy exploration. Despite limited freshwater access, improvements in desalination technologies could facilitate water consumption for electrolysers. Third, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Saudi Arabia, and Oman have made substantial investments exceeding US$69 billion in strengthening hydrogen infrastructure and have established partnerships with counterparts in Europe and Asia.[14] Consequently, hydrogen production costs in the Middle East are projected to decline significantly by 2030 (see Table 1).

These early policy ambitions have yet to translate into continuous investments and tangible infrastructural development. articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays and downscaling of the futuristic development housing it.
The NEOM Stadium was billed as an elevated arena in a glitzy 100-mile (160-km) steel and glass structure known as The Line, in turn part of the broader development known as NEOM.
NEOM was introduced about a decade ago as a centrepiece of de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030, an ambitious plan to diversify the economy and cut reliance on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of NEOM's owner the Public Investment Fund, confirmed in April that The Line was no longer a priority, and said it was not vital before 2030, the original delivery target for its first phase. He denied any projects had been cancelled.
However, according to two sources, plans to build the NEOM Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely.
NEOM and the Saudi government media office did not reply to requests for comment, while Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Sports redirected questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The Authority said "substantial delivery" of construction milestones for the event was already taking place, but did not address questions around the NEOM Stadium and costs. It shared images of some of the other stadiums under construction.
Riyadh developing 15 venues for 2034 World Cup
The 2034 World Cup is seen as a marquee event for Saudi Arabia, which under the Vision 2030 programme has invested heavily in sports via wealth fund PIF. The tournament will be the first time a single nation hosts the expanded 48-team format.
Riyadh is working to build or renovate 15 venues across five cities, as well as dozens of training facilities.
MEED Projects, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform whose team of analysts tracks tenders and projects in the region, puts the total value of the projects at $22.7 billion in data shared with Reuters.
According to MEED, NEOM's stadium is expected to cost $2.5 billion. It lists the projected 46,000-seat stadium in its data as "on hold".
The stadium has no listed completion date, according to the data, which describes the remaining stadiums and facilities as in various stages of development, with completion expected between 2026 and 2033.
Saudi Arabia is under increasing pressure from the Iran war, which has led to heavy disruptions to energy shipments and damage to critical infrastructure, with the kingdom facing attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis.
Last week, the Ministry of Finance said it expected a fiscal deficit this year wider than previously projected and a real GDP contraction of 3.6% following a drop in oil activities.
Pivot for giga-projects
The geographic distribution of the stadiums adds to the challenge of delivering the projects, a third source said. That could further be compounded by some projects set to host stadiums being delayed or downsized, such as The Line or Riyadh's New Murabba development, the source added.
In January Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia has suspended construction of The Mukaab, a colossal cube-shaped skyscraper at the centre of the New Murabba.
Reuters also reported last year that the PIF was pivoting from its focus on costly giga-projects to endeavours with more immediate financial returns, a strategy later articulated by Saudi officials.
Still, other projects for the World Cup are progressing. The Aramco Stadium in the eastern city of Al Khobar is set to be completed by the end of this year and host its first game in January, for which tickets are on sale.
Work on other planned stadiums is going ahead, a fourth source said.

articles.summary: Beyond tariffs: The US–Turkey trade relationship needs a bigger bargain  Atlantic Council
articles.full_text:
Turkey has much of what the United States wants from an economic-security partner, combining a strong manufacturing base with strategic geography and regional influence. Yet it faces a comparatively high tariff burden, and new risks stemming from its energy relationships with Russia and Iran.
The tension reflects a broader change in how Washington is using tariffs: not only to protect domestic industries, but to encourage trading partners to invest in the United States, align with US regulatory and economic-security priorities, and build more secure supply chains. The result is a trade system in which market access increasingly depends on a country’s contribution to US industrial and economic-security goals.
For Ankara, that means thinking beyond tariff relief. For Washingon, Turkey’s industrial capacity, strategic location, and access to important regional markets create the opportunity to turn a difficult trade relationship into an economic security partnership. A structured bargain linking tariff relief to greater bilateral trade, investment, and supply-chain security could advance the two countries’ longstanding $100 billion trade goal while deepening cooperation in strategically important sectors.
The evolution of US trade policy toward Turkey
During President Donald Trump’s first term, Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum, Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods, and the renegotiation of the North American Free Trade Agreement into the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement laid the foundation for an America First trade policy that, by the start of Trump’s second term, had evolved into a more integrated strategy linking trade policy with national security.
Turkey entered this environment through Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. In 2018, Turkish steel initially faced a 50 percent rate before reverting to 25 percent in 2019. In 2025, the United States expanded Section 232 coverage and raised the general steel and aluminum tariff rate to 50 percent before further restructuring the metals regime in 2026. Turkey exports more than $1 billion of steel annually to the United States, making steel a major source of friction.
Washington has since broadened both the legal authorities it uses and the objectives tariffs are intended to serve. In April 2025, a 10 percent tariff was imposed on Turkey as part of the initial “Liberation Day” tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), then the lowest rate applied to any major US trade partner. After the US Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, the White House imposed a temporary 10 percent import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration then turned to a broader use of Section 301 of the Trade Act.
In July, the US Trade Representative (USTR) finalized tariffs under its forced-labor investigations covering sixty economies, including Turkey, for not having imposed and effectively enforced strong enough prohibitions on goods produced with forced labor. Economies that adopted, or committed to adopt, qualifying controls received a 10 percent rate. Turkey and most other investigated economies received a 12.5 percent rate. Notably, Turkey was not among the sixteen economies potentially subject to additional tariffs under a second Section 301 investigation into structural industrial excess capacity.
Turkey’s strategic value and economic security exposure
Several major US trade partners, including Japan, the European Union, South Korea, and Switzerland, have negotiated arrangements that cap their combined most-favored-nation and forced-labor Section 301 tariff burden at 10 percent or 12.5 percent. Turkey has no comparable arrangement.
Exposure also varies by product. Goods already covered by Section 232 are generally excluded from the forced-labor Section 301 tariffs, while products outside the Section 232 regime may instead fall under the new Section 301 tariffs. Ordinary customs duties and, for certain products, antidumping or countervailing duties can raise the final cost even further.
Furthermore, Turkey’s exposure increasingly extends beyond traditional tariff policy. The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 allows for tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports from certain major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, potentially including Turkey, in addition to other applicable tariffs.
Iran poses an additional challenge because Turkey has historically balanced its strong commercial and energy connections with Iran against US sanctions. On September 4, the Treasury Department sanctioned a Turkish financial institution and two affiliates, accusing them of helping Iran evade sanctions and manage oil revenue.
At the same time, Turkey’s industrial base and geography give it potential value to US economic security objectives. Its economy spans automotive production, machinery, aerospace and defense, steel, energy equipment, and advanced manufacturing, while its integration into European value chains gives Turkish firms experience in sophisticated production networks. Its location also provides commercial connectivity across the Black Sea, the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa, positioning it as a potential partner in US efforts to diversify strategic supply chains and reduce dependencies.
That potential spans across sectors vital to Washington’s economic security agenda. Turkey could contribute in areas such as critical minerals, energy, defense, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure, and regional logistics. Closer economic ties would not eliminate Turkey’s strategic independence or ensure alignment with US policies, but they could deepen cooperation on shared priorities, including energy and trade routes, infrastructure, and regional economic projects.
The opportunity for a broader US–Turkey bargain
In 2025, US–Turkey goods trade reached about $36.8 billion, including a roughly $4 billion US surplus in 2025. Overall trade in goods and services has more than doubled since 2019, when Trump and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan established a target of $100 billion in bilateral trade, but remains well short of that ambition.
Turkey has no reciprocal trade agreement that offers a clear path toward preferential tariff treatment or deeper economic cooperation. For Ankara, tariff relief should therefore form part of a broader negotiating agenda. Turkey could offer greater market access for US companies, address longstanding trade tensions, strengthen customs and supply-chain enforcement, and deepen regulatory cooperation in exchange for more predictable tariff treatment. An interim trade arrangement, potentially drawing on elements of US agreements with Taiwan and Indonesia, could provide a framework for addressing these issues while building toward a deeper economic relationship.
Turkey’s Digital Services Tax (DST) illustrates the potential bargaining space. USTR previously found the tax discriminatory and burdensome to US commerce, but Turkey later agreed to remove it once the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development Pillar One framework entered into force, prompting USTR to terminate its planned retaliatory tariffs. With that process unresolved, Turkey has instead begun phasing down the tax, from 7.5 percent to 5 percent in 2026 and 2.5 percent in 2027.
Addressing the DST would not directly affect Turkey’s 12.5 percent forced-labor tariff, but could remove a source of friction in broader negotiations. USTR’s July 2026 Section 301 action against Brazil shows that digital trade concerns remain part of Washington’s reciprocal trade and enforcement agenda.
Washington, in turn, should consider what it can offer. Tariff accommodations (including on Section 232 steel tariffs) along with improved market access and targeted US financing and investment could draw Turkey more deeply into trusted US supply chains while encouraging domestic and allied sourcing.
The administration has already shown willingness to calibrate tariffs where they could undermine broader economic security objectives, including through exclusions for selected raw materials and domestically unavailable inputs. Targeted accommodations could similarly support US industrial and supply-chain objectives.
Turkey’s comparative advantage in such a bargain would not be in matching the scale of US investment pledges made by Japan or South Korea. It would be its industrial capacity, geographic reach, and ability to support diversification across strategically important regions.
Steel offers an obvious place to test that proposition, but any accommodation would also require confronting global excess capacity and transshipment risks. Turkey’s participation in the September 2026 Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity provides a potential foundation for addressing those concerns alongside the United States and other major steel-producing economies.
Any deeper economic partnership could therefore be reciprocal, though not symmetrical. Turkey can offer greater market access, regulatory cooperation, supply-chain safeguards, sourcing transparency, and access to industrial and regional networks. The United States can offer capital, technology, financing, strategic investment, and potentially more favorable tariff treatment.
A structured US–Turkey economic security partnership could bring these elements together and provide a more concrete framework for their shared trade ambitions while lowering economic frictions, enhancing Turkey’s integration into US and allied supply chains, and reinforcing shared interests across strategically important regions.
Leo Ayala is a vice president for global trade and supply chains at a Washington, DC-based geopolitical advisory firm. He previously served as an international trade specialist in the Office of Europe and Eurasia at the US Department of Commerce. The views expressed are his own.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW: Iraq's new oil freight strategy and the reinvention of crude trade - Business Upturn
articles.summary: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW: Iraq's new oil freight strategy and the reinvention of crude trade  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
The events surrounding the Strait of Hormuz in 2026 have shown that crude oil in the ground is not the same thing as deliverable crude. A barrel on the wrong side of a chokepoint is commercially very different from an identical barrel already aboard a vessel that can reach the buyer.
That distinction matters most in Iraq. Iraq has relied overwhelmingly on its southern export infrastructure around Basra, with buyers arranging the tankers to lift its crude. The Hormuz disruption has upended that model. Baghdad has had to contend with the physical risk of the strait, scarce tankers, soaring freight and insurance costs, and the discounts needed to persuade buyers to take on that risk.
Iraq has been testing alternatives. In late August, state marketer SOMO offered Basrah cargoes for ship-to-ship (STS) loading near Oman's coast, reportedly its first such tender. In September it tendered a two million barrel Basrah Heavy cargo for STS loading outside the strait, and the Oil Ministry confirmed a Qayara cargo routed beyond Hormuz. Iraqi crude has been offered at steep discounts at Basra, and moving the sale point outside Hormuz could let Iraq capture more of the value that traders and logistics providers had absorbed.
The latest step came on 3 October. The state-owned Iraqi Oil Tankers Company announced that it had moved two million barrels of Iraqi crude through the strait aboard a chartered very large crude carrier (VLCC), calling it the company's first such operation in decades. Reuters noted that Iraq had previously secured Iranian permission for its tankers to transit. The company is also working to buy its own specialised crude tankers.
On land, a one-year interim agreement signed with Türkiye on 1 August sets a transit capacity of 750,000 barrels per day on the Iraq–Türkiye pipeline to Ceyhan, though actual flows have been far lower. Baghdad is advancing plans for a Basra–Haditha–Kirkuk–Ceyhan line. In July it signed a memorandum with Syria to rehabilitate the Haditha–Baniyas pipeline to the Mediterranean, a project Syrian officials say could take about three years.
The result is an emerging Iraqi strategy built on optionality rather than a single export corridor. To understand what it means for commodities, freight and pricing, we spoke with Adv. Capt. Sandeep Saxena.
Q1. Is Iraq's decision to put two million barrels aboard a VLCC and move the cargo beyond Hormuz really a shipping development, or a fundamental change in how Iraq markets its oil?
Saxena: I would regard it primarily as a change in the commercial architecture of Iraqi oil marketing, with shipping as the mechanism.
For many years the model was straightforward. Iraq produced crude, SOMO marketed it, and buyers arranged the vessels to lift it from the southern terminals. A significant part of the post-sale transportation risk was effectively transferred to the buyer and the trader.
The Hormuz disruption exposed the weakness in that structure. The question was no longer whether Iraq had crude, but whether a buyer was willing and able to take delivery through a maritime environment of security risk, constrained tanker availability, exceptional freight rates and elevated insurance costs. Once that happens, the physical location of the crude becomes commercially decisive.
A barrel sold FOB at Basra is not economically equivalent to the same barrel placed on a vessel outside Hormuz. The latter is further along the logistical chain. The seller has assumed more transportation responsibility, but it has also gained greater control over destination, timing and the pool of potential buyers.
That is why the recent movement should not be dismissed as a one-off emergency voyage. Iraq is beginning to ask whether control over freight can increase the value of the commodity itself.
SOMO reportedly offered Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy at very substantial discounts while traders acquired crude at Basra and resold it outside the chokepoint. Its offshore sales were an attempt to capture some of the value that had accrued to intermediaries for assuming the logistics and risk. That is an important evolution in commodity marketing.
Q2. Why should a commodities professional care about the difference between selling oil at Basra and selling it outside Hormuz?
Saxena: Because in a crisis the point of sale stops being just a contractual location. It becomes a risk-pricing mechanism.
Take two barrels of identical Iraqi crude. One is sold FOB at Basra. The buyer must arrange a tanker, obtain insurance, accept the security exposure and absorb any delay or additional freight. The other is carried by the seller beyond the chokepoint and offered at a location where the security and freight profile is materially different. The crude is the same. The logistical risk attached to obtaining it is not, and that difference enters the price.
Reports indicated that SOMO offered significant discounts for Basrah crude because buyers were reluctant to assume the transportation risk, while offshore loading let Iraq contemplate retaining more of the value otherwise surrendered through discounts.
The commercial value of a barrel should increasingly be understood as the value of the molecule plus the cost, risk and reliability of delivering it to the refinery. That is a very different market from the one you see by looking only at Brent, Dubai or Oman benchmarks.
Q3. Are we seeing a new concept in crude trading, where freight itself becomes part of the commodity?
Saxena: In practical terms, yes.
Oil has always been influenced by freight, but freight has historically been treated as a separate component of delivered cost. Hormuz has shown that the distinction can become artificial during a major geopolitical disruption.
Reuters reported a record of roughly $1.27 million per day for the Middle East–China VLCC time-charter route in late September. Before the war, the long-run average was a small fraction of that. At those levels, transportation is no longer a secondary consideration. It becomes one of the principal determinants of whether a cargo is commercially attractive. For a two million barrel cargo, the difference is enormous.
The trader is no longer asking merely, "What is the crude worth?" The trader is asking, "What is it worth after freight, war risk, insurance, delay exposure, financing cost, demurrage risk, port costs, transhipment and the probability of disruption?"
That is why freight markets can influence physical oil prices so dramatically. In extreme circumstances, a cargo can be technically available but economically unavailable. That distinction is fundamental to commodities trading.
Q4. Does Iraq's proposed purchase of its own tankers mean Baghdad is trying to become a shipowner, or a more sophisticated commodity trader?
Saxena: I think the latter is closer to the strategic reality.
Owning tankers is not automatically advantageous. They require capital, technical management, crew, maintenance, classification, insurance, dry-docking, regulatory compliance and commercial employment. A government should not acquire ships merely because freight rates are high.
But ownership can create something more valuable than freight savings: control. A state exporter that owns or controls suitable tankers can decide when to lift cargo, where to position it, whether to hold it in transit, whether to sell at origin or destination, and how much freight risk to retain. That optionality can be worth a great deal in a crisis.
The Iraqi Oil Tankers Company has discussed acquiring specialised crude tankers, and officials have linked ownership to stronger export control and better financial returns. But Baghdad must avoid assuming that ownership equals strategic independence. A badly timed, poorly managed or excessively concentrated fleet can become another vulnerability. The right approach is a commercially disciplined fleet, not a politically attractive one.
Q5. Could the VLCC movement matter more for Iraq's pricing power than for its export volume?
Saxena: Absolutely.
Two million barrels is significant, but it cannot solve Iraq's export problem. According to its Ministry of Oil, Iraq averaged around 2.6 million barrels per day in September, well below the roughly 3.3 to 3.5 million before the war disrupted maritime flows.
The more important achievement is the change in bargaining position. When a buyer knows the seller can deliver crude beyond the most problematic part of the route, the buyer has less justification for demanding a very large discount simply for accepting Basra delivery. That is how logistics becomes pricing power.
If Iraq can repeatedly show that it has alternative lifting arrangements, offshore transfer capability and access to vessels, it changes the negotiating environment with traders and refiners. The objective should not be to move every barrel outside Hormuz, which would be expensive and inefficient. It should be to have enough alternatives that no buyer can price Iraqi crude as though the country has only one export route.
Q6. What is the hidden economic significance of ship-to-ship transfer outside Hormuz?
Saxena: STS changes the geography of the transaction.
In the conventional model, crude moves from a storage system to a terminal and onto a large tanker that takes it directly to the refinery. With STS, a cargo can be repositioned from a high-risk logistical environment into a lower-risk or more commercially attractive one. It also allows different vessel sizes: a smaller tanker can carry crude from the Gulf to a transfer area, where it moves to a larger vessel for the longer voyage. That is why shuttle systems have become so important across the Gulf.
But STS is not free of risk. It adds manoeuvring, transfer and operational exposure, along with weather, pollution, vessel compatibility, equipment, communications, liability and insurance issues.

articles.title: Israel’s innovation economy and the growth of new start-ups - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Israel’s innovation economy and the growth of new start-ups  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Israel has transformed itself into a global powerhouse of technological innovation, earning the well-deserved nickname "Start-up Nation." With over 6,000 active start-ups and a thriving ecosystem that spans cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and medical devices, this small country punches far above its weight on the world stage. The secret sauce combines elite military intelligence units, world-class universities, and a culture that celebrates risk-taking and failure. Investors from Silicon Valley to Tokyo recognize the unique value that Israeli founders bring to the table. Even in entertainment and digital platforms, Israeli developers push boundaries, much like the innovation and user experience found at best canadian online casino RocketPlay. The synergy between technological advancement and entrepreneurial spirit creates an environment where groundbreaking ideas become billion-dollar companies.
Key facts: Start-up Nation by the numbers
Israel's innovation economy continues to shatter records and defy expectations. Here are the most striking statistics that define this dynamic landscape:
- Israeli start-ups raised a record-breaking $25.6 billion in 2021, though 2026 projections show a stabilization at around $15 billion annually as the market matures.
- The number of active tech companies in Israel reached 6,653 by mid-2025, with approximately 1,500 new start-ups founded each year.
- Cybersecurity firms account for 30% of global private investment in the sector, with Israeli companies like Wiz and SentinelOne achieving unicorn status.
- The Wix headquarters in Tel Aviv employs over 3,000 people, making it one of the largest tech employers in the country.
- Israel boasts the highest density of start-ups per capita in the world, with one start-up for every 1,400 citizens.
- The government's Innovation Authority allocated $600 million in 2026 to support early-stage ventures and encourage corporate partnerships.
- Exits and IPOs generated $72 billion in value between 2020 and 2025, with companies like Monday.com and JFrog leading the charge.
What drives Israel's unmatched start-up velocity?
The military plays an unexpected but crucial role in shaping Israel's tech landscape. Elite units like Unit 8200 and Talpiot train young soldiers in cutting-edge cyber intelligence and software development. These conscripts graduate with technical skills and a network of contacts that often becomes the foundation for future ventures. Many of Israel's most successful start-ups trace their origins directly to military service, where solving complex problems under extreme pressure becomes second nature. The transfer of knowledge from defense to civilian applications creates a pipeline of innovation that no other country can replicate.
Universities contribute equally to this ecosystem. The Technion in Haifa and the Weizmann Institute in Rehovot produce graduates who rank among the world's most sought-after engineers and scientists. Research partnerships between academia and industry ensure that theoretical breakthroughs quickly translate into commercial products. The government's Office of the Chief Scientist provides matching grants for R&D projects, reducing the financial risk for early-stage founders. This combination of military training, academic excellence, and government support creates an environment where entrepreneurship thrives.
The culture itself encourages bold moves. Israeli society embraces questioning authority and challenging conventional wisdom. Start-up founders often describe the "chutzpah" factor as essential to their success. This willingness to take calculated risks reflects the determination and ambition that drive entrepreneurs to push boundaries and pursue major breakthroughs. Unlike more conservative business cultures, Israelis view failure as a learning opportunity rather than a stigma, which keeps the pipeline of new ventures flowing continuously.
The global impact of Israeli innovation
Israeli technology touches nearly every aspect of modern life, often in ways that go unnoticed. The Waze navigation app guides millions of drivers worldwide, while Mobileye's advanced driver-assistance systems make roads safer across continents. In healthcare, Given Imaging's pill cameras allow doctors to examine the digestive tract without invasive procedures. Every year, multinational corporations establish R&D centers in Israel to tap into this wellspring of creativity. Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Intel all maintain significant operations in Tel Aviv and Haifa, employing thousands of local engineers.
The cybersecurity sector deserves special attention. With cyber threats growing exponentially, Israeli firms lead the charge in protecting digital infrastructure. Companies like Check Point Software Technologies and CyberArk defend banks, governments, and enterprises from sophisticated attacks. The 2026 forecast predicts that Israeli cybersecurity exports will exceed $20 billion, cementing the country's position as the undisputed leader in this critical field. International partnerships and joint ventures multiply the impact of these innovations, creating a global network of technological cooperation.
The start-up ecosystem also benefits from a robust support infrastructure. Venture capital firms, accelerators, and incubators provide funding and mentorship at every stage of growth. OurCrowd, an equity crowdfunding platform, democratizes access to start-up investments, allowing individuals worldwide to participate in Israel's success story. The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange introduced new listing requirements in 2025 to attract high-tech companies, offering another exit path for founders. This comprehensive support system ensures that promising ideas receive the resources they need to scale globally.
Challenges and opportunities in a changing landscape
Despite its successes, Israel's innovation economy faces real challenges. The high cost of living in Tel Aviv pushes some start-ups to establish offices in smaller cities like Beersheba and Haifa, spreading economic benefits across the country. The shortage of skilled workers, particularly in AI and machine learning, creates intense competition for talent. Global economic uncertainty and changing investor sentiment require start-ups to demonstrate profitability sooner rather than later. These pressures force the ecosystem to evolve, emphasizing sustainable growth over rapid expansion.
However, new opportunities emerge from these very challenges. The government's 2026 initiative to integrate ultra-Orthodox and Arab citizens into the tech workforce expands the talent pool dramatically. Climate tech start-ups attract growing investment, addressing environmental concerns while creating economic value. The healthcare sector pivots toward digital health solutions, with telemedicine and remote monitoring platforms gaining traction. Israeli companies increasingly look to Asian markets, diversifying their customer base beyond the traditional focus on North America and Europe.
The rise of artificial intelligence reshapes the start-up landscape in profound ways. Israeli AI companies specialize in everything from natural language processing to computer vision, applying their expertise to industries as varied as agriculture, finance, and transportation. The integration of AI into existing products creates new revenue streams and competitive advantages. Investors recognize this trend, directing record amounts of capital toward AI-focused start-ups. The future belongs to companies that harness AI's transformative potential, and Israeli founders stand ready to lead this charge.
Conclusion: A resilient ecosystem built for the future
Israel's innovation economy demonstrates remarkable resilience and adaptability in the face of global challenges. The combination of military-grade discipline, academic excellence, and cultural fearlessness produces a start-up ecosystem that consistently outperforms expectations. As the world becomes increasingly digital and interconnected, Israel's technological contributions will only grow in importance. The same spirit that drives entrepreneurs to build world-changing companies also attracts global attention and investment. Whether you're an investor seeking opportunities or simply an observer of technological progress, keeping an eye on Israel's start-up scene offers endless fascination and potential. The next breakthrough could come from anywhere, but Israel's strong technological ecosystem makes it a leading source of future innovation.
