articles.title: 3 years on, Israel's Gaza genocide continues despite cease-fire
articles.summary: Gaza on Wednesday marks three years since Israel launched a genocidal war on the Palestinian territory, which continues to reel from unlivable conditions, daily killings by the Isr...
articles.full_text:
Gaza on Wednesday marks three years since Israel launched a genocidal war on the Palestinian territory, which continues to reel from unlivable conditions, daily killings by the Israeli military and being cut off from the rest of the world.
The situation there has improved little since a U.S.-backed cease-fire last October that was supposed to bring an end to the war and destruction has only been partially enacted.
The U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Tuesday that the truce has failed to provide stability or sufficient relief, urging all parties to fulfill their obligations to achieve a lasting peace.
"Last year's cease-fire brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace," Guterres said.
The U.N. chief also called on all sides to advance to subsequent stages of the truce based on the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
"It is time for the cease-fire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law," he said, calling for a "political path to lasting peace across the whole region."
"Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity, and aspirations fulfilled," Guterres said.
He added that Palestinians in Gaza have faced a "massive loss of life, displacement and destruction," without specifying their death toll.
"Their suffering, too, demands an end, now," Guterres added.
Gaza authorities and international nongovernment organizations have raised alarm that Israel has continued its atrocities in the coastal enclave, killing 1,454 Palestinians and injuring 5,090 others since the cease-fire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
Even Tuesday, at least three Palestinians were killed and several others injured by Israeli army fire.
The latest killings pushed the total Palestinian death toll in Israel’s genocide past 74,000, most of them women and children, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Earlier Monday, France-based Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has warned that Israel was continuing its genocide in Gaza and was "progressively asphyxiating" the region.
In a statement, MSF said the conditions for the people's survival were being "systematically destroyed" through sustained violence, "deliberate" blockade of essential supplies and the destruction of health care as well as infrastructure.
"In the past year, the physical trapping of people in Gaza has been made increasingly definitive by the establishment of Israel's Yellow Line," the French medical charity said, noting that the line has continued to move west, "squeezing people into a smaller and smaller area."
Meanwhile, global hunger watchdog IPC says more than 1.2 million people face acute hunger in Gaza despite a major scale-up of aid operations after the cease-fire.
In an August report, it cited data showing that an average of 227 trucks a day carried humanitarian and commercial supplies into Gaza from the cease-fire to the end of May – less than half the minimum 600 trucks stipulated in the Gaza plan.
Aid agencies say Israel is blocking essential items, including metal tent poles, engine oil and spare parts, from entering Gaza, claiming Hamas could use them for military purposes.
In addition, Gaza also suffers from overcrowding and limited access to clean water, sanitation, shelter and healthcare that contribute to the spread of disease, said MSF.
It also pointed to the dramatic deterioration of access to health care over the past three years as hospitals run out of basic supplies and patients are unable to access essential medicines and treatment.
"Restrictions on essential supplies, such as engine oil and spare parts, are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances and water systems running, with generators already breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced," the statement said.
Three years on, Palestinians are scavenging in the rubble of wrecked buildings for materials to prop up tents and other shelters after around 82% of buildings in the Gaza Strip were damaged in Israel's genocide, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS) said Monday.
The war-displaced population now faces yet another winter with little to no shelter and dwindling aid due to Israeli stranglehold.
Over the weekend, displaced people in the southern Gaza Strip appealed for tents, blankets and basic supplies. They warned that shelter shortages and dwindling humanitarian aid could leave thousands exposed to rain, cold and strong winds.
Ahmed Hassan al-Najjar, who oversees Fash Farsh in Khan Younis, told AA that 35 displacement camps there shelter 6,000 families, or about 40,000 people.
He said residents were facing shortages of tents, tarpaulins, food parcels and medical supplies and called for urgent assistance.
"We are heading into winter and we need tarpaulins, tents, food and health supplies so we can withstand the heavy rain and winds," Iyad Zomor told Turkish Anadolu Agency (AA).
"Our tents are torn and our stomachs are empty. Do not leave us to the unknown," said one of the protesters.

articles.title: Israeli army fires at, kills unarmed civilians in S. Syria: Reports
articles.summary: Israeli army investigations have found that three people its forces shot in two separate incidents in southern Syria Monday were unarmed, according to Israeli media reports. In the...
articles.full_text:
Israeli army investigations have found that three people its forces shot in two separate incidents in southern Syria Monday were unarmed, according to Israeli media reports.
In the first incident, the Israeli army announced early Monday that it had killed a "suspect" who allegedly attempted to infiltrate a military post inside the security zone occupied by Israel in southern Syria.
According to the Israeli army’s account, the young man continued attempting to enter the site despite being fired upon. A soldier then fired at him again, killing him. The army later confirmed that the young man was unarmed.
The second incident occurred Monday afternoon, when Israeli forces spotted two people on a motorcycle heading toward a military post in the area the army refers to as the "buffer zone."
The army said its forces carried out what it described as an "arrest procedure for a suspect," which involved firing live ammunition at the motorcycle and resulted in one of the two people being wounded.
The army arrested both men and transferred them to Israel for interrogation, while the wounded man was taken to an Israeli hospital for treatment. The army confirmed later that neither man was armed. No Israeli soldiers were injured in either incident.
The Israeli account of the incidents has been framed in terms of what it claims are "security concerns," with calls "to strengthen security in the Golan and allocate the necessary resources, including maintaining a presence in the buffer zone and the Mount Hermon area."
The two incidents came amid continued Israeli military aggression against Syria. On Oct. 2, Israeli patrols entered the villages of Hamidiyah and Bir Ajam in the Quneitra countryside, searched a number of homes and abducted a young man.
The Sijil Center documented 280 Israeli violations in Syria in September, including ground incursions, with Quneitra governorate recording the highest number.
Since the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israel has continued to violate the 1974 Disengagement Agreement through repeated incursions by its forces beyond the buffer zone adjacent to the Golan Heights, extending as far as Mount Hermon, which separates Lebanon from Syria. Israel has also announced its intention to establish a so-called "demilitarized zone" in southern Syria.
Syria, meanwhile, is demanding Israel’s withdrawal from its territory, stressing that all measures taken by Tel Aviv are null and void and have no legal effect under international law.

articles.title: CIA reportedly raises civil war, state collapse alarm for Israel
articles.summary: A classified CIA assessment has warned that deepening political, economic and social divisions could put Israel at risk of civil war or state collapse, according to a report publis...
articles.full_text:
A classified CIA assessment has warned that deepening political, economic and social divisions could put Israel at risk of civil war or state collapse, according to a report published Monday.
The assessment, titled "Fracture From Within," was prepared in August by the CIA’s Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging prevailing intelligence assumptions, Drop Site News reported, citing two U.S. sources familiar with its contents.
The CIA did not respond to the outlet’s request for comment.
The assessment points to a volatile mix of pressures ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election, including economic strain, rising military spending, anger over exemptions from compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews and escalating violence by Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank.
It also identifies Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s fight to remain in power as a source of further political and constitutional tension.
Years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran have deepened existing divisions, according to the report, as soldiers return from prolonged combat, many suffering serious psychological trauma.
The military draft dispute has emerged as one of Israel’s sharpest internal fault lines, with resentment growing over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men following repeated reserve mobilizations.
The assessment also points to Israel’s growing international isolation, including eroding support in the U.S., as another factor that could deepen internal instability.

articles.title: Top Democrat is investigating Jared Kushner’s financial investments after CNN report - CNN
articles.summary: Top Democrat is investigating Jared Kushner’s financial investments after CNN report  CNNJared Kushner Denies His Israeli Diplomacy Might Benefit His Tel Aviv Business Interests  ForbesKushner pushes back on CNN report about Israeli investments tied to military  The HillKushner could cash in on Israel’s war economy as he oversees negotiations  MS NOWGeraldo Rivera and Joe Borelli Throw Down Over Jared Kushner in CNN Brawl  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
A top Democratic lawmaker is seeking information on Jared Kushner’s financial investments following a CNN investigation last week that found his private equity firm is the largest shareholder in an Israeli company backing businesses involved in Israel’s military campaigns.
Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee, sent Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, a letter on Monday saying Democrats on the committee were “investigating the unprecedented and dangerous ways in which President Trump and his family have profited directly from their access to power.
“…I request detailed information about your business dealings in the Middle East to understand whether your significant financial gains have come at the cost of Americans’ safety and security, ” the California representative wrote.
The letter is yet another sign that House Democrats are poised to investigate President Donald Trump’s family members’ business dealings overseas and in the US, should they retake the majority in the midterm elections this fall.
An attorney for Kushner dismissed Garcia’s criticisms and sought to draw attention to the congressman’s own holdings in investments scrutinized in CNN’s report on Kushner – Phoenix Financial, an Israeli financial services firm which counts Affinity Partners as its biggest investor, and Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer.
“Rep. Garcia’s letter is a masterclass in irony: A member of Congress questioning a private citizen for having an interest in the same stock in which the member also holds an interest,” the attorney said in a statement to CNN. “Jared has no role in deciding what Phoenix buys or sells. But if that doesn’t matter to Rep. Garcia, he should begin by investigating himself.”
Garcia’s most recent disclosure forms indicate his pension plans are managed through the California Public Employees’ Retirement System and California State Teachers Retirement System. Both plans hold stock in Phoenix Financials or Elbit Systems.
A spokesperson for Garcia said Kushner’s attorney was trying to “deflect” from his client’s own conduct, adding the congressman does not trade stocks and, like the millions of other public employees in the pension plan, does not have any control over the fund and cannot opt out.
Kushner “makes millions with no accountability all while he travels the Middle East on behalf of his father in law,” said Sara Guerrero, Garcia’s spokesperson.
“The apparent conflict of interest between Affinity Partners’ investments and your work in the Middle East, and in particular the potential for corrupt dealmaking given those competing interests, demands congressional oversight and accountability,” Garcia’s letter stated.
CNN’s investigation raised questions about potential conflicts of interest between Kushner’s volunteer role as a peace envoy to the Middle East, and his firm’s financial investments. Kushner’s attorney did not address his client’s role as a negotiator on behalf of the Trump administration.
As part of the review into Kushner’s financial holdings, CNN used Israeli financial transparency laws to trace investments made by Phoenix Financial, a Tel Aviv-based firm that Kushner’s Affinity Partners doubled its stake in last year, shortly before Trump returned to the Oval Office. CNN’s reporting specifically excluded Phoenix’s investments through retirement accounts and focused on insurance holdings instead.
Those records, which include only some of Phoenix’s holdings, show Phoenix has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into Elbit Systems. Phoenix also holds stakes in at least eight other companies providing equipment for the Israeli military ranging from drones and warships to demolition machinery, CNN found.
All nine companies identified by CNN saw their stock value climb last year, with many stating the war in Gaza had driven demand for their businesses.
Affinity doesn’t directly hold a stake in the nine companies CNN identified – but it does stand to reap rewards when Phoenix makes a profit. Kushner described Phoenix as Affinity’s “best investment” in September 2025.
CNN found no indication that Kushner’s actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed. Kushner’s attorney told CNN his client has “never participated in or directed Phoenix’s decisions” on where to invest.
A day after CNN’s reporting, Kushner posted a rare response on X, calling CNN’s story “deeply misleading.” Kushner did not point to any inaccuracies in the piece in his post.
“Misleading stories will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace. That work is too important,” Kushner wrote on X.
Garcia referenced Kushner’s social media post, writing “despite your denial of improper behavior, the fact remains that you have been allowed to hold a position of enormous power and responsibility, exempt from financial disclosure requirements and outside oversight.”
In addition to CNN’s report, the New York Times published a story detailing additional “intermingling” between Kushner’s volunteer diplomatic role and his businesses, as it related to the war in Ukraine.
US talks with Russia to end that war have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar deal selling oil assets from one of Russia’s biggest energy companies to a group of investors with ties to Steve Witkoff and Kushner, the two main negotiators for the Trump administration, according to the Times.
A spokeswoman for Witkoff told the Times he “has no conflict of interest or financial stake in this matter” and said his work for the US administration is undertaken “at his own expense.”
Kushner’s attorney did not respond to CNN’s inquiry about this reporting.
Garcia and other Democrats have for years demanded answers from the White House and Trump’s family about concerns over “apparent influence peddling and quid pro quo deals” and whether foreign money is being used “to buy access to the President and influence American policy.”
In March, Garcia and Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden specifically requested information from the White House about Affinity Partners’ fundraising in the Middle East – Kushner secured a $2 billion investment for his firm from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in 2021— in light of Kushner’s government work.
Neither Kushner nor Affinity Partners responded to the congressmen’s earlier request.
The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is the main investigative committee in the House but the minority party requests from lawmakers on the committee are voluntary and can be ignored without legal consequences. Subpoenas can only be authorized by the committee chair or by committee vote. If the balance of power shifts as a result of the midterm elections in November, Democrats would be able to open an official investigation.
After Republicans won the House in 2023, the Oversight Committee, the Judiciary Committee and the Ways and Means Committee opened similar investigations into Hunter Biden’s business dealings overseas and alleged he was profiting from his father’s presidency.

Moody’s Ratings said Saudi Arabia’s preliminary budget statement points to renewed spending restraint despite a wider deficit in 2026, adding that the fiscal recovery planned for 2027 supports its view that prudent fiscal management will remain a key factor in spending and borrowing decisions.
In a report, the ratings agency highlighted that a large near-term deficit, by itself, does not change its fundamental assessment of Saudi Arabia, noting that the Kingdom’s established fiscal strengths support its rating.
Moody’s expects GDP to contract by 3.3% in 2026 before growing 8.5% in 2027, compared with the government’s forecasts for a 3.6% contraction followed by growth of around 12.8%, respectively. It explained that its forecasts reflect weaker non-oil growth and a more moderate recovery.
The medium-term debt trajectory remains broadly consistent with previous forecast of an increase to 40% of GDP by the end of the current decade, provided that fiscal recovery is achieved. The effectiveness of government spending restraint will be a key factor determining the debt trajectory and its credit implications, it added.
Moody’s also said the pre-budget statement raised the expected deficit for 2026 to SAR 245 billion, equivalent to 4.9% of GDP, from SAR 165 billion, or 3.3%, in the original budget, indicating weaker near-term fiscal performance.
It noted that the deficit revision reflects spending exceeding the original budget rather than lower-than-budgeted revenue. Expected spending rose 9% to SAR 1.435 trillion from SAR 1.313 trillion, while revenue increased 4% to SAR 1.190 trillion from SAR 1.147 trillion.
Higher oil prices have cushioned the impact of lower production and exports, Moody’s said, but prolonged trade disruptions and additional spending have limited the fiscal improvement it previously expected.
For 2027, the agency expects spending to decline by around SAR 43 billion, or 3%, to SAR 1.392 trillion, while revenue is forecast to increase 1% to SAR 1.202 trillion. This would reduce the expected deficit to SAR 191 billion, or 3.6% of GDP.
It expects the fiscal deficit to remain at levels equivalent to 3.1% of GDP in 2028 and 3.3% in 2029.
Moody’s confirmed that government financial assets, including central bank deposits and the relatively liquid assets of the Public Investment Fund (PIF) after deducting its direct debt, amounted to around 18% of GDP at end-2025. Readily accessible deposits at the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) also exceeded 9% of GDP.
It added that strong access to capital markets provides Saudi Arabia with fiscal flexibility, while the authorities’ track record in controlling spending, implementing revenue measures, and reprioritizing projects supports policy credibility.
The agency believes that reprioritizing investments linked to Saudi Vision 2030 could preserve fiscal space while economic diversification continues. Focusing resources on projects with strong returns would likely help reconcile growth objectives with spending restraint.
Moody’s identified the duration and severity of the regional conflict as the main downside credit risk. It noted that continued disruption to the East-West Pipeline, Red Sea terminals, or shipping routes through the Bab El-Mandeb Strait could weaken oil revenues and external accounts, potentially outweighing the benefits of higher prices.
It added that prolonged insecurity could weigh on tourism, investor confidence, and the outlook for diversification, while substantial revenues would likely provide only limited protection against sustained damage to export capacity.
Moody’s also said insufficient and sustained fiscal recovery, a significant increase in debt, depletion of reserves, or continued damage to export capacity and non-oil growth are not included in its baseline scenario, but would likely increase downside pressure on Saudi Arabia’s credit profile.

ERBIL, Kurdistan Region of Iraq - Iraqi Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad on Tuesday announced that the country is set to ban the Israeli-developed Waze GPS navigation app by the end of December, accelerating a timetable that was initially set to prohibit the software's usage in 2027.
"We have decided to revoke our earlier decision to ban the Waze app at the start of 2027 and instead move the effective date to the end of this coming December," Sanad said in a statement on his Facebook account.
Founded as FreeMap Israel in 2006 and acquired by Google in 2013, Waze was developed by three entrepreneurs who had served in the Israeli military's Unit 8200, which is responsible for signals intelligence collection and cyberwarfare.
The platform says it is available in 50 languages and can be used "anywhere there is cellular/GPS reception."
Under the terms of Iraq's 2022 law on Criminalizing Normalization with the Zionist Entity, those who establish "any diplomatic, economic, political, military, security, cultural, or any other kind of relationship" with Israel may face life imprisonment or a death sentence, with the legislation having underpinned Baghdad's efforts to restrict ties with the state.
In 2017, Iran moved to block access to Waze in the country on account of its Israeli origins and potential counterintelligence risk, a fate that the messaging app Viber met three years prior on the same grounds.

articles.title: 3 Energy Stocks Positioned for Extended Iran-War Volatility - TradingView
articles.summary: 3 Energy Stocks Positioned for Extended Iran-War Volatility  TradingView

The prolonged Iran conflict has reshaped global energy markets beyond a simple rise in crude prices. Middle Eastern oil flows have started recovering as producers find alternative ways to move barrels, but shipping disruptions, high freight costs, tight refined-product supplies and pressure on liquefied natural gas (LNG) availability continue to keep the market unsettled.
Brent crude recently moved back around $100 per barrel after a sharp pullback, highlighting how quickly prices are reacting to changes in Gulf exports, military developments and shipping conditions. This volatility makes company-specific positioning increasingly important.
Companies with limited exposure to disrupted Middle Eastern assets, strong LNG export capacity or diversified global operations may be better placed to navigate an extended conflict. Against this backdrop, Chevron Corporation CVX, Cheniere Energy, Inc. LNG and Shell plc SHEL stand out for different reasons.
Energy Markets Remain Under Pressure
The global oil market has adjusted to the disruption faster than initially expected. Middle Eastern crude exports have rebounded as producers increasingly rely on pipelines, shuttle tankers and ship-to-ship transfers to move barrels around affected shipping routes.
However, the recovery has been uneven. Refined-product markets remain tight, particularly diesel, while higher freight costs and limited tanker availability continue to complicate global energy flows.
LNG has also become an important part of the supply story. Disruptions to Qatari production have increased the strategic value of suppliers outside the Middle East, particularly U.S. exporters. Meanwhile, companies with strong U.S. oil production can participate in elevated global prices while avoiding heavy dependence on Persian Gulf supply routes.
Chevron: Diversified Production Supports Resilience
Chevron is well positioned to benefit from stronger crude prices while limiting direct exposure to the Middle East. Much of the company’s production growth is coming from the United States and Guyana.
Chevron has built a large presence in the Permian Basin, while its acquisition of Hess added a 30% interest in Guyana’s Stabroek Block. Guyana has emerged as a major source of new oil supply outside the Middle East, strengthening Chevron’s geographic diversification.
The Hess acquisition, combined with continued growth from U.S. operations, has expanded Chevron’s overall production base. The company also maintains a sizable downstream business, giving it exposure to stronger refining conditions when global fuel inventories tighten.
This positioning matters during a prolonged conflict. Higher crude prices can support upstream earnings, while Chevron’s limited dependence on Middle Eastern production reduces the risk that regional disruptions erase those gains.
Strong cash generation also provides flexibility to fund projects, manage debt and maintain shareholder distributions through volatile commodity cycles.
For investors, Chevron’s appeal therefore extends beyond higher oil prices. Its expanding U.S. and Guyana operations provide meaningful production exposure while keeping direct conflict-related operating risks relatively contained. CVX currently carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).
You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.
Cheniere Energy: U.S. LNG Gains Strategic Importance
Cheniere Energy offers a different way to participate in the changing energy landscape. Rather than relying mainly on crude prices, the company benefits from its position as a leading U.S. LNG exporter.
That role has become more important as disruptions to Middle Eastern LNG production encourage buyers to diversify supply.
Cheniere Energy recently completed the Corpus Christi Stage 3 project, increasing LNG production capacity across Corpus Christi and Sabine Pass by more than 20% to roughly 56 million tonnes per annum.
The added capacity arrives at an opportune time. Reduced Qatari LNG availability has increased demand for reliable suppliers capable of delivering cargoes to Europe, Asia and other major consuming regions.
Cheniere Energy is also pursuing additional LNG capacity through further development opportunities at Corpus Christi and Sabine Pass, subject to regulatory and investment approvals.
The company had already raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA and distributable cash flow outlook before the latest tightening in global LNG supplies. Its expanded infrastructure and contracted customer base provide a strong foundation to serve growing demand.
For Cheniere Energy, the prolonged Iran conflict creates an opportunity tied more to energy security than short-term gas-price movements. If buyers continue seeking geographically diversified supplies, U.S. LNG could become increasingly important, potentially supporting additional long-term contracts. Cheniere Energy currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).
Shell: Integrated Model Provides a Cushion
Shell faces greater direct Middle Eastern exposure than Chevron or Cheniere Energy, making its investment case more complicated.
The company has significant operations in Qatar and elsewhere in the region, and the conflict has already affected some assets. Damage to one processing train at the Pearl gas-to-liquids facility highlights the operational risks associated with prolonged regional instability.
However, Shell’s diversified global business provides several potential offsets.
The company operates across upstream oil and gas, LNG, refining, chemicals and commodity trading. This integrated structure allows stronger performance in one segment to help cushion weakness elsewhere.
Shell’s LNG trading capabilities are particularly valuable during periods of supply disruption. The company can redirect cargoes across regions and respond to changing price differentials, helping it capture value from market volatility.
Its refining operations provide another buffer. Tight diesel and fuel markets can support refining margins, adding an earnings stream beyond upstream production.
Still, Shell carries greater conflict-related risk than Chevron because of its Gulf exposure. Continued instability could affect production and project schedules. Yet its diversified portfolio reduces dependence on any single region or commodity. SHEL carries a Zacks Rank #3 at present.
Why These Three Stocks Stand Out
Chevron, Cheniere Energy and Shell provide three different ways to navigate the same geopolitical disruption.
Chevron combines higher oil-price exposure with growing production in the United States and Guyana. Cheniere Energy benefits from the rising strategic importance of U.S. LNG as buyers seek alternatives to Middle Eastern supply. Shell carries greater Gulf exposure but can rely on its global LNG, trading, refining and upstream businesses to offset part of the impact.
The key advantage shared by all three is operating flexibility. As the Iran conflict continues to reshape global trade routes and energy availability, companies with diversified production, export infrastructure and multiple earnings streams may be better positioned to remain resilient through an extended period of volatility.

articles.title: Israel and India Elevate Health Partnership with Landmark AI and Digital Health Commitments - Republic World
articles.summary: Israel and India Elevate Health Partnership with Landmark AI and Digital Health Commitments  Republic World
articles.full_text:
India and Israel are deepening health cooperation with a focus on artificial intelligence, digital healthcare and biotechnology. A planned Joint Working Group on Health will explore innovation and best practices, building on existing cooperation in medical research, pharmaceuticals and healthcare.
Show Quick Read
India and Israel have opened a significant new chapter in their health cooperation, elevating their bilateral relationship to a “Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity” during the Modi-Netanyahu summit in Jerusalem on February 26, 2026. At the heart of this upgraded partnership lies a forward looking commitment to transform healthcare through artificial intelligence and digital innovation.
The leaders called for the first ever Joint Working Group on Health to convene in early 2026, explicitly framing the collaboration around healthcare innovation, AI and digital transformation. Both Prime Ministers agreed to deepen cooperation through sharing best practices and fostering institutional partnerships between the two countries.
This marks a meaningful evolution from the traditional focus of India-Israel health cooperation, which has historically centered on professional exchange, pharmaceutical regulation and hospital infrastructure development.
The foundation for this new chapter rests on a solid framework. India and Israel signed an Agreement on Cooperation in Health and Medicine in December 2020, replacing an earlier 2003 agreement.
Advertisement
That agreement established cooperation in exchange and training of medical professionals, regulation of pharmaceuticals and medical devices, development of climate resilient hospitals under a “Green Healthcare” banner and joint research initiatives. The February 2026 commitment builds upon this foundation by directing cooperation toward the digital frontier.
Israel’s health technology ecosystem provides a natural complement to India’s ambitions. Israel is widely recognized as a global hub for medical innovation, with particular depth in AI diagnostics, medical imaging, remote monitoring and personalized medicine.
Advertisement
In November 2025, India’s Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal highlighted Israel’s remarkable density of innovation, noting the country has “one startup with every 1,000 people,” and emphasized medical technology devices as a priority sector for collaboration.
Israeli health-tech breakthroughs continue to demonstrate the ecosystem’s vitality, including the world’s first successful transplantation of a fully 3D bio printed, cell based corneal implant performed at Rambam Health Care Campus in late 2025.
The strategic logic of this partnership is clear. Israel offers frontier innovation capabilities, while India brings unmatched market scale, manufacturing capacity and a rapidly digitizing health infrastructure.
The February 2026 joint statement recognized this complementarity, emphasizing the transformative potential of cooperation in digital healthcare, biotechnology and advanced pharma. The leaders also welcomed the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in Artificial Intelligence, alongside an agreement to advance AI-led education through institutional collaboration.
Looking ahead, the collaboration is expected to address critical areas including AI-enabled health systems, remote monitoring, cybersecurity in healthcare and data driven clinical decision making. The planned India-Israel Centre of Excellence in Cybersecurity, discussed during the summit, would support the protection of digital health records and connected medical devices as healthcare systems become increasingly digitized.
It is important to note that the Joint Working Group on Health represents an agreed commitment to convene rather than a program already delivering outcomes. Similarly, the medtech startup bridge discussed by officials in late 2025 was described as being explored rather than launched.
The concrete results of this elevated partnership will depend on what the first working group meeting actually delivers. Nonetheless, the February 2026 summit has established a clear direction bringing India-Israel health cooperation into the same digital register as the rest of their bilateral relationship, with AI and innovation at its core.

RIYADH: Gulf economies could rebound sharply in 2027, with the World Bank forecasting 10.3 percent growth if the Iran conflict does not escalate this year.
The organization made the claim on the basis that oil production and shipping return to normal from early 2027, with trade, tourism and domestic activity also looking to bounce back following the disruption caused by the US-led ward.
The impact of the conflict, which has led to extensive disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, is likely to see Gulf Cooperation Council economies contract by 4.3 percent in 2026, according to the report.
Output in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan is also projected to decline by 2.1 percent this year, following growth of 3.3 percent in 2025.
“If the conflict subsides by the end of 2026, growth in the MENAAP region, excluding Iran, is projected to rebound to 7.8 percent in 2027, driven largely by the recovery of hydrocarbon production and exports. However, a regional recovery is not guaranteed and will require sustained policy efforts,” said the World Bank.
Saudi economy to rebound to 7.9%
The World Bank forecast Saudi Arabia’s economy to contract by 2 percent in 2026 before rebounding by 7.9 percent over the following 12 months.
The Kingdom has been partly shielded from the impact of the oil export disruption, thanks to the East–West Pipeline, which carries crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
Commenting on the Kingdom’s economic growth in 2027, Thomas Kuruvilla, managing partner of Arthur D. Little Middle East and India, said that the Kingdom is entering the rebound next year with a broader economic base than in previous oil cycles.
“Construction, logistics, business services, tourism and hospitality should all benefit from stronger activity, while continued investment under Vision 2030 can reinforce their longer-term development,” said Kuruvilla.
He added: “The important question for 2027 is how effectively the oil recovery translates into greater private-sector activity, productivity and investment. If that happens, the rebound can accelerate diversification rather than simply lift growth cyclically.”
Kuruvilla expects the Kingdom’s tourism sector to gain substantial benefits from the economic recovery next year, as the nation has built a substantial pipeline across hospitality, entertainment and destination development.
“Destinations that establish distinctive propositions and repeat demand will be particularly well placed to benefit from the recovery,” added Kuruvilla.
Wider outlook
According to the World Bank report, the Middle East and North Africa economy is projected to contract by 2.8 percent in 2026, following 3.4 percent growth in 2025.
The World Bank projects Qatar’s gross domestic product growth to reach 26.7 percent in 2027 as liquefied natural gas production resumes, while Kuwait’s economy is expected to grow 22 percent as oil exports normalize.
In the UAE, economic growth in 2027 is projected at 9.5 percent, followed by Bahrain at 4.2 percent and Oman at 3.4 percent.
Kuruvilla said that greater regional stability and a recovery in economic activity should help boost investor confidence across the region.
“Evidence of commercially attractive opportunities, stronger private-sector cash flows and increasing risk-sharing with private investors would signal that the rebound is becoming a broader and more durable re-rating of the GCC region,” said Kuruvilla.

Daijiworld Media Network - Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia, Oct 6: Fresh attacks in the Middle East injured three people at two airports in Saudi Arabia, while an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City killed one person and severely injured another, as violence in the region showed no sign of easing.
Nearly three years after Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the conflict has continued to affect several parts of the region, including Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen. Israel also began commemorations on Monday to mark three years since the deadliest day in the country's history.
Saudi Arabia said on Tuesday that two of its airports had been attacked, leaving three people lightly injured. The attacks came hours after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they had fired missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said airports in Najran and Jizan were hit on Monday, causing damage to both facilities. The authority did not identify those responsible. The statement came after the Houthis announced attacks on Saudi oil facilities, airports and military bases on Monday.
Saudi Arabia and its allies supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government have launched a military campaign to reclaim Houthi-controlled territory near the southern tip of the Red Sea, amid concerns over disruptions to oil exports from the region.
In Gaza, an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City killed one person and severely injured another, according to health officials at Shifa Hospital. The Israeli military said it had targeted a militant near the municipal park, a densely populated area of the Gaza Strip, but provided no further details.
The strike was the latest deadly attack since a ceasefire took effect nearly a year ago. More than 1,460 Palestinians have been killed since then, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, whose figures are generally considered reliable by the United Nations and independent experts.
Meanwhile, Israel is observing a week of mourning to mark three years since Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack. Commemorations began on Monday, corresponding to the anniversary in the Jewish calendar, with further events scheduled for Wednesday, the anniversary according to the international calendar.
During the attack, militants killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages, triggering a war that later spread across the region. The attack left deep trauma in Israel, particularly in communities near the Gaza border.
Many residents in those communities continue to struggle with a loss of security after nearly three years of war, which has devastated much of Gaza and killed about 74,000 Palestinians, according to health officials in the territory.
The latest developments underline the continuing impact of the conflict across multiple fronts, with renewed attacks in Saudi Arabia, further deaths in Gaza and Israel marking three years since the October 7 attack.

articles.summary: Countries with the Largest Natural Gas Reserves  وردنا
articles.full_text:
Natural gas reserves are pivotal in the global energy landscape, affording countries the ability to meet domestic demands, bolster energy-related industries, and export to international markets. A significant share of these reserves is concentrated in countries with massive fields in Asia and the Middle East.
A select group of countries tops the list of those with the largest natural gas reserves, with some playing crucial roles in the liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade and pipeline transport.
Rankings of nations vary depending on data year and sources, thus relying on confirmed reserves is recommended for international comparisons.
Which Countries Have the Largest Gas Reserves?
According to available confirmed reserve data, Russia leads in natural gas reserves globally, followed by Iran and Qatar. The U.S., Turkmenistan, Saudi Arabia, and China also rank among the countries with significant global reserves.
1. Russia
Russia holds the world’s largest natural gas reserves, estimated at 47.2 trillion cubic meters as of the 2024 Eni energy report. Major reserves are found in Siberia, historically making Russia a primary gas supplier to European and Asian markets via pipelines.
2. Iran
Iran ranks second with reserves nearing 34 trillion cubic meters. The South Pars field, shared with Qatar, is a major gas source. Iran’s substantial reserves position it as a key player globally, although sanctions and infrastructure issues impact its production and export capabilities.
3. Qatar
Qatar holds the third spot with reserves around 23.8 trillion cubic meters according to 2024 data. It’s a powerhouse in the global LNG market, with the North Field forming the foundation of its gas industry and promising additional reserves for future exploitation.
4. United States
The U.S. has significant natural gas reserves, approximately 18.4 trillion cubic meters as per 2024 Eni data. Beyond its reserve size, the U.S. is a major natural gas producer, with shale gas contributing to its prominent position in the global energy sector and boosting LNG exports.
5. Turkmenistan
Turkmenistan ranks among the leading holders of gas reserves with around 14 trillion cubic meters as of 2024 data. The Galkynysh field is a critical source, with pipeline exports, particularly to Asian markets, being vital to its economy.
6. Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia has substantial natural gas reserves and is developing new resources like unconventional gas at the Jafurah field. Aramco announced an addition of 15 trillion cubic feet of raw gas to confirmed Jafurah reserves, with higher total field resource estimates.
7. China
China holds significant gas reserves and is also a leading producer and consumer globally. Gas is increasingly crucial in China’s energy mix, spurred by expanded gas infrastructure and LNG facilities.
8. United Arab Emirates
The UAE has considerable natural gas reserves, aiming to boost local self-sufficiency and meet industrial and electrical demand. The nation is investing in gas production, processing, and development of onshore and offshore fields.
9. Venezuela
Venezuela is among countries with large gas reserves, alongside possessing one of the largest oil reserves globally. Despite immense resources, actual production is affected by investment, infrastructure, and economic factors.
10. Nigeria
Nigeria ranks prominently with vast gas reserves, supporting its LNG production and exports. Contemporary comparisons suggest over 5 trillion cubic meters of confirmed reserves, marking it as Africa's major gas player.
What is the Largest Natural Gas Field in the World?
The South Pars/North Field is the world’s largest gas field, a geological offshore field shared between Iran and Qatar in the Persian Gulf, boasting about 51 trillion cubic meters of reserves. Its Iranian section is called South Pars, while Qatar's is known as the North Field.
Is Russia the Country with the Most Gas Reserves?
Yes, Russia is the leading country in confirmed natural gas reserves per various international databases. Eni’s 2024 data suggests Russian reserves at 47,152 billion cubic meters, compared to Iran’s 33,988 billion and Qatar’s 23,831 billion cubic meters. Some databases might reflect slightly varied figures due to updated estimates and discoveries.
What is the Difference Between Gas Reserves and Production?
An extensive gas reserve doesn’t equate to high annual production. Reserves refer to economically and technically extractable quantities under current conditions and knowledge, while production indicates the actual gas extracted over a period. Hence, a country might top reserve rankings but not production. The U.S., Russia, Iran, and China are top producers, differing from reserve rankings.
Why Do Some Countries Have Massive Gas Reserves?
Large gas reserves are influenced by geological factors formed over millions of years, including large sedimentary basins and suitable gas formation and entrapment conditions. Exploration and technology impact reserve size, with new discoveries or efficient techniques boosting extractable resource amounts.
What is the Economic Importance of Gas Reserves?
Gas reserves significantly contribute to revenue for producer nations, especially with infrastructure enabling pipeline exports or LNG conversion. Gas supports local industries, electricity generation, and petrochemicals, thus its importance extends beyond export, providing a long-term energy source and industrial support.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia to ABANDON their £2BILLION one-of-a-kind World Cup stadium plan to host football at 350 metres above ground level amid spiralling costs - Daily Mail
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia to ABANDON their £2BILLION one-of-a-kind World Cup stadium plan to host football at 350 metres above ground level amid spiralling costs  Daily Mail
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia to ABANDON their £2BILLION one-of-a-kind World Cup stadium plan to host football at 350 metres above ground level amid spiralling costs
FIFA announced Saudi Arabia as the host nation for the 2034 World Cup almost two years ago but the organisers are already running into serious issues - with the construction of one of their biggest venues set to be scrapped.
Plans for one of the hosts' most ambitious venues for 2034, a futuristic elevated football stadium, have been scrapped, worrying fans and pouring £2billion down the drain in the process.
The NEOM stadium was sold as a one-of-a-kind sporting arena as a part of the 100-mile-long steel and glass structure known as The Line, a mirrored linear smart city meant to house nine million people, the original focal point of Saudi Arabia's NEOM mega project.
NEOM themselves own a Saudi Pro League Side, NEOM FC, that employ ex-Premier League stars such as Alexandre Lacazette, Said Benrahma and Malang Sarr.
NEOM was introduced nearly a decade ago as a key part of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030. The 2034 World Cup is seen as a marquee event for the country and under Vision 2030 Saudi Arabian investment in football over the last four years, via the wealth fund PIF, has been immense.
Eye-watering sums have been spent on in bringing in top players and coaches as well as building footballing infrastructure in preparation for the 2034 World Cup, with 15 stadiums in total being built or renovated.
Saudi Arabia have found success in some of their footballing investment but the NEOM stadium will be one to forget
Plans for a stadium in Neom saw a pitch 350m above ground and integrated into The Line
Plans for The Line, a 200 kilometre long row of skyscrapers, look set to be scaled back
The tournament will be the first time a single nation hosts FIFA's new 48-team format and Riyadh have been working to transform 15 venues across five cities alongside dozens of training facilities.
MEED, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform, lists developments on the NEOM stadium as 'on hold' and the stadium has no listed completion date in their data. The remaining stadiums in the wider project are listed in various stages of development, with completion expected by 2033 at the latest.
But with plans for one of the most expensive and key venues seemingly shelved, questions will be raised over whether Saudi Arabia will be prepared come 2034.
Saudi Arabia also looks to be under increasing pressure from developments in the Iran war and has had to deal with heavy disruptions to critical infrastructure as well as energy shipments.
These issues will only add to Saudi Arabia's ever-growing costs and continue to hinder the Kingdom's efforts to prepare the nation for hosting the world's biggest sporting event in just under eight years time.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia quietly shelves 2034 World Cup stadium as doubts emerge over flagship £1.9bn project - Football Ground Guide
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia quietly shelves 2034 World Cup stadium as doubts emerge over flagship £1.9bn project  Football Ground Guide
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's ambitious plans for a futuristic World Cup stadium have reportedly been shelved as doubts continue to grow over the wider NEOM development.
The £1.9bn project was intended to become one of the most spectacular venues at the 2034 World Cup.
Why Saudi Arabia have shelved ambition ‘sky stadium' for 2034 World Cup
The proposed NEOM Stadium was planned as a 46,000-seat arena elevated inside The Line, the futuristic 100-mile development which has been a centrepiece of Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 plans.
However, Reuters reports that plans for the stadium have now been shelved indefinitely, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
The stadium was expected to cost around $2.5bn (£1.9bn), with construction industry analysts MEED Projects listing the project as “on hold” with no completion date.
The development has faced growing uncertainty after NEOM governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan confirmed earlier this year that The Line was no longer a priority, although he insisted that projects had not been cancelled.
Saudi Arabia is still pressing ahead with its wider World Cup preparations, with 15 stadiums planned across five cities alongside numerous training facilities. The total value of the stadium projects is estimated at $22.7bn.
However, the reported shelving of the NEOM Stadium adds to evidence of a broader shift away from some of Saudi Arabia's hugely ambitious giga-projects towards developments offering more immediate financial returns.
FGG says: Saudi Arabia's World Cup plans face an important reality check
The NEOM Stadium was arguably the most eye-catching of Saudi Arabia's proposed 2034 World Cup venues, making its reported shelving a significant development.
The tournament is still eight years away and plenty of time remains to deliver the required infrastructure, but abandoning such an ambitious project demonstrates just how dramatically Saudi Arabia's priorities appear to be changing.
For football fans, this may ultimately mean a less futuristic World Cup than originally envisaged. However, with other stadium projects continuing, the wider tournament plans remain firmly on track for now.

articles.title: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, UAE back railway linking Central Asia to Pakistan’s seaports - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, UAE back railway linking Central Asia to Pakistan’s seaports  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates have signed a memorandum of understanding to jointly develop a new railway corridor linking Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan, potentially giving Central Asian countries access to Pakistan’s seaports on the Arabian Sea.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The information was shared with The Media Line by the office of Afghan government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid.
Afghan media outlets Ariana News and Pajhwok Afghan News have also reported the development, while Kazakhstan’s Prime Minister’s Office confirmed the signing of the memorandum.
The proposed Central Asia-South Asia railway would pass through Uzbekistan and Afghanistan before reaching Pakistan.
According to Kazakhstan’s Prime Minister’s Office, the transport ministries of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure signed the memorandum to expand cooperation in international transport, trade, logistics and investment.
Under the agreement, the three countries will conduct technical and economic studies, analytical assessments and feasibility work on the required railway infrastructure and related facilities. They are also considering establishing a joint effort to examine the project’s technical, economic and financial aspects.
Afghanistan could serve as land route between Central, South Asia
The main objective is to strengthen transport links between Central and South Asia, expand trade and create new investment opportunities. The railway could offer Central Asian countries an alternative route for imports and exports through Pakistan’s seaports.
Since the corridor would pass through Afghanistan, its completion could provide the country with an opportunity to play a greater role in regional trade and cargo transit.
Afghanistan could serve as a land route for transporting goods from Central Asia to South Asia and connecting regional markets through Pakistan’s ports.
Afghan economic analyst Jannat Fahim Chakari stated that the project could create opportunities for Afghanistan to earn transit revenues and benefit from other economic activities.
However, he said such benefits would depend on effective implementation of the agreements and detailed assessment of the project.
Afghanistan’s Deputy Minister of Economy, Abdul Latif Nazari, said the railway could strengthen Afghanistan’s transit role and make it an important link between Central and South Asia.
Beyond transit fees, the corridor could generate activity in freight transport, warehousing, customs, logistics and other businesses. However, these benefits would depend on construction, border arrangements, trade policies and efficient transportation systems.
Project to face myriad of challenges
Experts say the project will face challenges including financing, construction costs, cross-border connectivity, administrative coordination, security concerns, customs procedures and border facilities, particularly amid the deteriorating and strained relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
The memorandum remains an initial step toward assessing the project’s technical and economic feasibility. Its future will depend on the findings of the studies and subsequent decisions by the countries involved.
Pakistan has expressed support for the railway project, with Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal recently calling for an accelerated feasibility study and a joint mechanism with Uzbekistan to seek international financing.
However, Pakistan’s Ambassador to Russia Faisal Niaz Tirmizi has said that instability in Afghanistan has effectively stalled Islamabad’s regional transport connectivity projects, highlighting the security and political challenges facing the proposed route.

articles.title: Some nations have deployed space weapons. Here's what issues are worrying experts - PBS
articles.summary: Some nations have deployed space weapons. Here's what issues are worrying experts  PBSTurkey condemns deployment of space weapons after American weapons reach orbit  Middle East EyeSpace Weapons: Disclosure Isn’t Enough for Deterrence  CSIS | Center for Strategic and International StudiesSpace Force weapons may signal shift in US defense strategy: Ross Coulthart  NewsNationAP Business SummaryBrief at 12:01 p.m. EDT  www.pmg-ky3.com
articles.full_text:
VIENNA (AP) — Air Force Secretary Troy Meink made headlines recently by confirming the United States has deployed weapons in space. He did not, however, detail what the weapons were, how they work or if they were targeting other objects in space.
It's not just U.S. efforts regarding space weapons that remain shrouded in mystery.
Here's a look at issues that concern experts:
What we know about weapons in space
Meink, speaking at a defense conference, said the U.S. has fielded "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," referring to U.S. forces. It remains unclear which type of weapon Meink was referencing.
Such resources as the 2026 Global Counterspace Capabilities Report, published by the nonprofit Secure World Foundation and based on publicly available information, help provide an overview of potential space weapons.
The report lists five categories of counterspace capabilities. It examines systems being developed by 13 countries, among them the U.S., Russia, China, India, Australia, France, Iran, and Israel.
These include satellites designed to maneuver near, inspect, disable, or destroy spacecraft. The report also examines ground, air, or sea-launched missile interceptors designed to destroy satellites kinetically.
Furthermore, the report highlights electronic warfare, such as jamming, in addition to lasers or high-power microwaves meant to blind or damage satellite sensors. The report also lists cyber operations targeting space networks.
Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the foundation, which advocates for the peaceful use of space, said the existence of various satellites and their physical location in orbit is fairly transparent but their capabilities and intended uses are harder to understand.
For example, the Vienna-based U.N. Office for Outer Space Affairs supports transparency in space by maintaining a register which links each object to its responsible country. States who signed on to a 1976 agreement are required to provide information on launches by governments and private companies as well as the general function of the space object, but are not required to provide details on their purpose.
As an example of something that could be used for both military and non-military purposes, it became known in 2021 that China had tested a satellite with a robotic arm that can maneuver to a system, grab it, and move it out of orbit. In 2022, China used such a system for the first time to tow one of its dead satellites out of orbit.
Furthermore, the U.S. warned two years ago that Russia was developing a new space-based, anti-satellite weapon, though the White House said the danger wasn't imminent at the time.
Then-White House national security spokesman John Kirby declined to comment on whether the weapon was nuclear capable, but did say it would violate the Outer Space Treaty.
Russia denied developing such a new capability.
The Outer Space Treaty is a product of the Cold War
The Outer Space Treaty is the main international agreement that establishes the rules and norms for how countries explore and use space. In addition to Russia, the U.S., China and all other nuclear-armed nations are party to the treaty.
Article IV states that parties "undertake not to place in orbit around the earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner."
The treaty also declares that space is a global commons that can be used for only peaceful purposes.
The treaty was concluded in 1967 during the Cold War when the U.S. and the Soviet Union were both racing to explore space, and conducted a series of nuclear tests in orbit.
At the time, space looked radically different.
Jonathan McDowell, a retired astronomer from the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, has been tracking satellite launches for more than four decades.
By the end of 1967, 128 satellites were in orbit and communicating with Earth, according to McDowell. At the time, all satellites were the product of state-backed, public projects. This is compared to what McDowell says are approximately 16,810 functioning satellites today — many of which are from companies such as SpaceX's Starlink network.
In 1962, the U.S. exploded a series of atomic bombs in space as part of Operation Fishbowl. The first one, the Starfish Prime test, was launched from an atoll southwest of Hawaii. The explosion caused an artificial radiation belt that destroyed several satellites and partially knocked out street lights and phone lines in Hawaii.
Likewise, the Soviet Union conducted nuclear tests in space as part of Project K between 1961 and 1962. The tests caused electrical grid failures, disabled phone lines and triggered a fire that destroyed an entire power plant in Kazakhstan.
The trials demonstrated the immense risk that atomic explosions in space pose to civilian infrastructure and communication on Earth, prompting the superpowers to seek an agreement that would ban nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in space.
There is a loophole
Analysts argue the treaty fails to address some of the challenges of modern times.
Jessica West, a senior researcher at Project Ploughshares, a Canadian peace and security research institute, said the legal framework governing space needed to be "fundamentally changed."
She said that while the Outer Space Treaty acts like a "constitutional foundation" that remains relevant and applicable, the international community has not done the "hard work" to build a legal structure around the treaty, especially when it comes to improving verification mechanisms for space activities and expanding principles to banning conventional weapons in space.
Michelle Hanlon, executive director of the Center for Air and Space Law at the University of Mississippi School of Law, agreed, saying there is a "gap" in the treaty when it comes to barring conventional weapons.
There's no consensus on what counts as a weapon
International efforts to negotiate a new framework banning all weapons in space have stalled because there is no agreement on what counts as a space weapon, among other things, according to Samson.
A lot of the capabilities are "dual use," meaning they can be used for civilian and military purposes, which makes it difficult to define what constitutes a weapon, she said.
"You can get up close to a satellite to refuel it, but you can also get up close to a satellite to release objects at it, shine a laser at it, or try to jam it," Samson said.
The discussions on banning weapons come at a time when the U.S. under President Donald Trump has placed a growing emphasis on space.
In 2019, during his first term, Trump created the Space Force as a separate military branch. In his second term, he has announced the "Golden Dome" missile defense system, which includes plans to put weapons in space.
Attempts by Russia and China to introduce a new treaty to prevent the placement of all weapons in space have hit a wall, in part due to the lack of a definition. Additionally, Washington says it ignores ground-based anti-satellite missiles that when used create massive amounts of dangerous space debris.
In November 2021 Russia launched such a missile to destroy a defunct Soviet-era satellite, creating more than 1,500 pieces of debris that increased risk to U.S. and Russian astronauts aboard the International Space Station and China's Tiangong space station.
With progress on the full treaty apparently stalled, international negotiations have shifted their focus to discussing responsible behavior in space, such as avoiding the accumulation of space debris.
The U.S. weapon could be non-kinetic
Samson said the U.S. has had a policy of avoiding the accumulation of space debris for many years because the debris can interfere with space flight safety and harm the U.S. self interest.
She also said that for the same reason there is a possibility that the space weapons Meink referenced could be non-kinetic weapons such as jammers.
Space debris is generated not only by kinetic space weapons but also when satellites collide and get smashed into countless fragments and smaller particles that travel at high velocity and are capable of destroying or damaging more spacecraft.
"If you start having collisions causing more debris, and more debris causing more collisions, you run the risk ... of this irreversible cascading effect," said Steven Freeland, who is emeritus professor of international law at Western Sydney University as well as professorial fellow at Bond University.
According to the European Space Agency, there are about 46,950 pieces of debris that are regularly tracked by space surveillance networks in Earth's orbit.
Based on statistical models, the agency estimates there are millions more smaller pieces of space junk circling Earth's orbit.

articles.title: Libya parliament speaker ousted after 12 years amid power shift
articles.summary: Libya’s parliament removed its longtime speaker on Tuesday after 12 years in office, ousting a key ally of east-based Khalifa Haftar in a move analysts said could signal a shift in...
articles.full_text:
Libya’s parliament removed its longtime speaker on Tuesday after 12 years in office, ousting a key ally of east-based Khalifa Haftar in a move analysts said could signal a shift in the country’s political balance.
MPs voted to replace Aguila Saleh with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, the parliament's spokesman announced on X.
Libya has been beset by violence and instability since the overthrow of Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.
It remains divided between the U.N.-recognized government in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Haftar.
Haftar's camp relies in particular on the parliament, which sits in the eastern city of Benghazi under their control.
Saleh, 82, has long been considered a staunch ally of the Haftar clan, but he appeared to be weakened as Haftar's sons, in particular Saddam Haftar, consolidated their positions.
Emadeddin Badi, an analyst at the London-based Chatham House, said: "Aguila Saleh appears to be the latest casualty of Saddam Haftar's drive to centralize decision-making in eastern Libya and bulldoze his way into a political role."
His removal comes as a U.S. initiative aimed at reviving the political process and unifying Libya's institutions is under discussion.

articles.title: Christa Pike awake, speaking after surviving execution attempt
articles.summary: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital after surviving the state’s attempt to execute her, her attorneys said Tuesday. "Against all odds, Chris...
articles.full_text:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital after surviving the state’s attempt to execute her, her attorneys said Tuesday.
"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital "who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her."
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalized Tuesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as they attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn't kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team, said the development "bodes well for a good recovery." But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her.
"She's still in the ICU," he said. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well."
Pike's attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.
The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I'Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.

Russia is closely tracking NATO statements about preparations for a potential attack by Moscow and remains vigilant amid heightened tensions with the alliance, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday.
"So, we hear what is being said, but, as the saying goes, we keep our guard up,” Lavrov told a news conference in Moscow after talks with Bendito Freitas, the foreign minister of Timor-Leste.
Lavrov said Moscow is focused on fulfilling the objectives set by President Vladimir Putin for the war in Ukraine, including preventing threats from its Western neighbors.
He also referred to recent tensions over Kaliningrad, saying Putin made it clear that any attack on the semi-exclave or another part of Russia would receive a response.
"When we issued a very clear statement in response to threats from Baltic and other NATO members-who have gotten out of hand-to attack the Kaliningrad region, we were immediately assured by both NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and the US Permanent Representative to NATO (Matthew) Whitaker that the bloc has no plans to attack Russia-nor could it-and that NATO is, after all, a defensive alliance,” he said.
On Afghanistan, Lavrov said Russia regretted that participants in the latest Moscow Format consultations failed to adopt a final document because of tensions between Kabul and Afghanistan.
He claimed the dispute was linked partly to the presence of ISIS (Daesh) militants in both countries, and called for an end to interference by countries from outside the region.
"I have no doubt whatsoever that both Afghanistan and Pakistan are interested in normalizing relations. Russia is doing its utmost to facilitate the resolution of both persisting and newly emerging problems," he said.
Lavrov described his talks with Freitas as "highly productive” and said the two sides discussed expanding cooperation in energy, mining, fisheries and tourism.
He said Russia was ready to increase energy supplies to the Southeast Asian country and expressed support for expanding educational and law enforcement cooperation.
The ministers also discussed cooperation through ASEAN and developments in the Asia-Pacific region, with Lavrov criticizing Western efforts to create exclusive bloc-based structures outside the ASEAN-centered framework.
Lavrov said they also discussed Middle East, Iran, and the war in Ukraine. He said Russia and Timor-Leste would prepare for events to mark the 25th anniversary of diplomatic relations in May 2027.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the ministers held a "substantive” exchange of views on bilateral issues, including deepening political dialogue, expanding trade, economic and humanitarian cooperation and strengthening the legal framework of their relations.
Lavrov said Freitas also discussed key international and regional issues and urged closer coordination between Russia and Timor-Leste within the U.N. system and the Russia-ASEAN dialogue partnership, it said.

articles.title: India opposition mounts protest after 130M deleted from voters list
articles.summary: India's opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police Tuesday during a protest march demanding the election chief's resignation over large-scale voter list revision...
articles.full_text:
India's opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was briefly detained by police Tuesday during a protest march demanding the election chief's resignation over large-scale voter list revisions.
Gandhi, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress Party, was standing on a police barricade and waving the national flag, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Officers detained him along with other lawmakers but released them soon after.
The revision of voter lists has drawn criticism over alleged irregularities in the decision-making process, with opposition politicians accusing the election commission of acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Critics also say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalized and minority communities, especially Muslims.
The Election Commission of India has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, saying the revision process is aimed at ensuring the accuracy and integrity of electoral rolls.
On Tuesday, opposition members began a march from parliament towards the commission's headquarters, but were stopped by a heavy police presence.
Gandhi and his lawmaker sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra later camped inside the public radio's offices adjacent to the election commission.
"The country has been hijacked by Narendra Modi through vote theft," Gandhi told reporters from behind the iron gates of the public radio building.
"What has been done to our country is called treason. Nobody is going to escape."
Modi's party has defended the drive.
"Some opposition parties, particularly the Congress, are making a concerted effort to change the government and install Rahul Gandhi in power," party spokesman Sambit Patra told reporters Tuesday.
"They are deliberately attacking India's democracy and constitutional institutions."
The protest is part of a wider campaign against revision of electoral rolls, reignited by a report last month by The Indian Express newspaper.
The report said that two of the election commission's three members had formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions linked to the revision and that the names of 130 million citizens had been deleted since the exercise began in 2025.
Protests began Friday, demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down.
"Gyanesh, it's done, bro," placards read at the protest Tuesday, alongside signs alleging electoral manipulation.
Opposition leaders pressed their demands for greater transparency, alleging that changes to the voter rolls could disenfranchise eligible voters.
Kumar has not commented publicly.
The election commission says the revision exercise is intended to identify fraudulently registered voters and prevent "foreign illegal immigrants" from voting.
The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical political movement that emerged online in May and succeeded in its campaign to oust the then education minister, has called for "mass mobilization" in the capital Saturday.
Major student groups aligned with left-wing parties have also said they would join Saturday's protest.
India's Supreme Court on Monday ordered the government and the election body to explain decisions linked to the revision exercise. Another hearing is expected to be held next week.
