articles.title: Separatists win in French-speaking Quebec, eye Canada exit
articles.summary: Quebec’s separatist Parti Québécois returned to power after winning Monday’s provincial election but failed to secure a majority, setting up a minority government as the party push...
articles.full_text:
Quebec’s separatist Parti Québécois returned to power after winning Monday’s provincial election but failed to secure a majority, setting up a minority government as the party pushes for another referendum on independence from Canada.
The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decade but denies it the majority it sought, forcing the separatists to rely on opposition parties even as they try to revive Quebec’s independence debate.
The party was on track to win nearly 60 seats as the final votes were counted, falling short of the 64 needed for a majority in Quebec’s 127-member National Assembly, the provincial legislature. A minority government means PQ will need support from opposition lawmakers to pass key legislation and survive confidence votes.
St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that voters had denied his party a majority. "Quebecers elected the Parti Québécois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message,” he said.
He has pledged to hold another referendum on independence, though he has said he would wait until U.S. President Donald Trump is no longer in office.
St-Pierre Plamondon framed independence as essential to preserving Quebec’s French-speaking identity, saying it was a "question of survival” for a French-speaking population that represents only a small fraction of North America. He said Quebec "just wants to exist on its own like other countries of the world” and that a referendum would allow Quebecers to decide their own future.
"I continue to dream and visualize that country,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. "That dream will be realized one day.”
He also sought to reassure Canadians outside Quebec. "The project for independence is not about excluding you,” he said. "Quebec will never change its geographical position, so we have an interest in working together.”
Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the "difficult result.” The CAQ, which entered the election with 79 seats, was shut out of the legislature, and Fréchette lost her own seat in Trois-Rivières.
But the PQ's victory does not mean most Quebecers support leaving Canada.
"This was not an election about independence, which is not popular in Quebec right now, but about getting rid of the CAQ, the party in power since 2018,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
Support for independence remains at about 30%, low by historical standards, he said. Béland said the minority result is likely welcome news for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government because it could make it harder for the PQ to prepare for and eventually call an independence referendum.
The PQ would face opposition from both the Liberals and Conservatives, whose leaders have said they would fight efforts to hold a sovereignty referendum. Québec solidaire, another pro-independence party, could hold the balance of power and potentially support the PQ on a referendum.
Carney congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and signaled that Ottawa would work with the incoming separatist government. "Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada,” Carney said. He said the two governments would work together to support businesses and workers affected by U.S. tariffs, create jobs and build housing.
Still, Béland said a separatist government in Quebec poses a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching elsewhere in Canada.
The Quebec result comes two weeks before Albertans vote Oct. 19 on whether to hold a referendum on separation from Canada.
"Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Béland said.
Quebec voters have twice rejected sovereignty, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.
Quebec, which is about 80% French-speaking, already has significant autonomy. The province of 9.1 million collects its own income tax, has immigration policies favoring French speakers and has laws giving the French language priority over English.
Even with the PQ victory, Trump’s tariffs and 51st-state rhetoric have complicated the separatist argument by stirring Canadian nationalism and giving some French-speaking Quebecers another reason to value remaining part of Canada.
Trump’s tariffs and repeated threats against Canada became a defining issue in the 2025 federal election, helping lift Carney’s Liberals to victory after the party had trailed badly before Trump returned to office.

articles.title: Thousands joining French school protests met with teargas, arrests
articles.summary: Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools Tuesday as students, teachers and parents held their largest demonstration yet against staff shortages and dilapi...
articles.full_text:
Police fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools Tuesday as students, teachers and parents held their largest demonstration yet against staff shortages and dilapidated classrooms.
In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs marked with "The state has killed national education" and other messages, in largely peaceful rallies. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.
But in Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.
"There is such a gap between the elites and us," said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.
The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide, presenting a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's cash-strapped government at a time when it faces strong economic headwinds.
The High School Students Union said more than half of France's high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.
"We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," said Roberta, another recent high-school graduate at a protest outside Paris' prestigious Henri IV school.
Schools were facing a list of problems from water leaks to rat infestations, she added.
The government has responded to the demonstrations with riot police.
Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.
France's Interior Ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said, without specifying the crimes.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu's office.
A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France Monday. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade.
"They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters," said Omar Slaouti, a high school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris.
"If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake," he added.
Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and Le Pen's National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests. LFI denies the accusation.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students' leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.
Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government's words were not enough. "That's all fine and dandy, but that's not what's going to change the daily lives of our children," she said.
Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.
The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France's growing debt pile, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push bond yields higher. The yield on France's 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.
The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right euro-skeptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring's election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.

articles.summary: A Ukrainian drone barrage, involving approximately 650 aircraft, targeted the Moscow region overnight, killing two people and damaging dozens of residential buildings, Russian auth...
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian drone barrage, involving approximately 650 aircraft, targeted the Moscow region overnight, killing two people and damaging dozens of residential buildings, Russian authorities said Tuesday.
Most of the drones were destroyed by air defenses at long range, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on Telegram. He said 105 drones were destroyed as they approached the Russian capital.
In addition to the two deaths, nine people were injured in the attack, according to Andrei Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region. It was not initially possible to verify these figures.
Vorobyov said 47 residential buildings had been damaged. Local reports said a fire had broken out in a warehouse in the village of Litvinovo.
The drone attacks continued into the morning, Sobyanin said, forcing Sheremetyevo Airport, the largest in the country, to suspend operations temporarily.
If the Russian figures on the number of drones shot down are accurate, they would point to a major Ukrainian attack.
Citing eyewitnesses, the Kyiv Independent reported that an oil production facility around 40 kilometers from Moscow was targeted.
Russian sources said the facility in the village of Konstantinovo is the region's largest reservoir and a key hub for Moscow's fuel supply. No official statement has been made regarding the target.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russia's oil industry to hit energy exports that provide important revenue for Moscow's war effort.
Ukraine has been defending itself with Western support against Russia's full-scale invasion for more than four and a half years and regularly targets sites deep inside Russian territory as part of its defense.
Russia, meanwhile, systematically attacks targets across Ukraine with drones and missiles, killing civilians and damaging homes and critical infrastructure.
At least six people were killed by Russian aerial bombs in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv Monday, according to authorities.
Investigators said 59 people were injured, while rescue workers continued searching the rubble of a residential building for possible further victims.
Also Tuesday, unidentified drones hit two commercial ships in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria, sinking one of the vessels, the government said.
While the sailors from the sunken ship were missing, those from the second ship were rescued, Rumen Nikolov, head of the local rescue operations in Varna, was quoted as saying by the BNR public radio.
Rescuers were scouring the area for the missing sailors, about 150 kilometers (90 miles) east of the coastal city of Byala, the radio said.
The government said it would convene an emergency meeting later Tuesday to discuss the strikes.
According to the Maritime.bg specialist site, the ship that sank was flying under a Togo flag.
The other ship was flying under a Palau flag, with 18 crew members evacuated by a Bulgarian ferry after the strikes.
Tuesday's strikes came a day after Romania reported that a grain ship had caught fire and sand near its coast, with two crew members killed, in an attack Ukraine blamed on Russia.
Türkiye's Chamber of Maritime Commerce (IMEAK) said last month that since the start of the war, 226 civilian and commercial vessels have been attacked in the Black Sea, the vast majority this year.

Former German intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason, according to media reports, in a case that could rank among the country's largest spy scandals.
Bild newspaper and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported Tuesday that federal prosecutors are investigating Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, from 1998 to 2005, and a second suspect.
According to Bild, the suspicions include obtaining state secrets, treason and espionage for a foreign power.
The investigation was launched after the discovery of an alleged leak of intelligence reports intended for the chancellery, Bild said.
The newspaper said Hanning paid a former member of the BND leadership staff for classified information and allegedly "planned to resell it" as part of his consulting work.
Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported that Hanning was supplied with secret material from the service years after he left office by his former office director. Investigators are examining whether he passed those secrets to foreign powers, the newspaper said.
It described the case as potentially one of the largest espionage affairs in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany.

articles.title: Gaza truce yet to deliver security, needs full commitment: UN chief
articles.summary: U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Tuesday that the Gaza cease-fire has failed to provide stability or sufficient relief, urging all parties to fulfill their obligation...
articles.full_text:
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Tuesday that the Gaza cease-fire has failed to provide stability or sufficient relief, urging all parties to fulfill their obligations to achieve a lasting peace.
"Last year's cease-fire brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace," Guterres said in a statement, ahead of the third anniversary of Oct. 7 incursion that triggered Israel's genocidal war.
The U.N. chief also called on all sides to advance to subsequent stages of the truce based on the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
"It is time for the cease-fire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law," he said, calling for a "political path to lasting peace across the whole region."
"Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity, and aspirations fulfilled," Guterres said.
Addressing the origins of the conflict, Guterres condemned the Hamas incursion that caused 1,200 deaths in Israel and took 251 hostages.
He also said Palestinians in Gaza have faced a "massive loss of life, displacement and destruction," without specifying their death toll.
"Their suffering, too, demands an end, now," Guterres said.
Israel's two-year genocidal war on Gaza killed more than 74,200 people, mostly women and children, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.
Israel, which still controls most of Gaza, refuses to withdraw its soldiers until Hamas' disarmament has been verified.
Hamas, for its part, has advocated for gradual disarmament rather than immediate and unilateral surrender of its arsenal.
The Israeli army has killed 1,454 Palestinians and injured 5,090 others since the cease-fire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since the 2023 incursion, Israel has waged military attacks on several fronts, notably invading southern Lebanon in the name of confronting Hezbollah and launching war against Iran in late February alongside the United States.
